items.title: From reporting to reasoning: Getting enterprise data ready for AI agents
items.description: AWS Quick User Group DC inaugural meetup recap Many organizations are asking how to move beyond static reporting dashboards and begin using generative and agentic AI. But before an AI agent can answer questions or help teams act, it requires a trusted data foundation. Figure 1: AWS Quick User Group DC inaugural meetup, October 2026 On Wednesday, October 7, 2026, data leaders, developers, and practitioners gathered at the AWS Skills Center in Arlington, Virginia, for the AWS Quick User Group DC meetup. The session brought together founders, software engineers, and enterprise leaders, among them a team from Financial Independence Group (FIG). Attendees explored practical strategies for modernizing legacy architectures, preparing structured data for agentic workflows, and automating routine tasks with no-code tools. User groups like this provide a forum for peer-to-peer learning and collaborative problem-solving. The event offered attendees an inside look at how organizations are putting AWS Quick to work to drive productivity gains. What’s new with AWS Quick: Agents, skills, and connectors For many in the room, this meetup was a first look at what agentic AI looks like in practice with AWS Quick. Figure 2: Arun Ganesan presenting what’s new with AWS Quick The meetup kicked off by exploring the latest product capabilities across AWS Quick, focusing on its evolution into a unified AI assistant for work. Rather than functioning solely as a traditional business intelligence visualization tool, AWS Quick unifies analytics, natural-language interaction, and multi-step task orchestration. AWS Quick agents and skills : Turn natural-language questions into multi-step reusable actions that aid in decision making across enterprise data. Third-party connectors : AWS Quick includes built-in integrations that connect tools like Salesforce, Slack, Google Drive, and Microsoft 365, breaking down data silos. Unified workspace : A cohesive environment that bridges research, automated visual generation, and business artifact creation (presentations, documents, and spreadsheets) directly where users work. Real-world innovation: Moving to AI analytics and agentic systems The core of the day highlighted a real-world customer journey showing how one enterprise is rethinking its data architecture so AI agents can work from governed, trusted data. Financial Independence Group: Innovating at the pace of technology Vanessa Gonzalez, Vice President of AI at Financial Independence Group (FIG), shared how FIG keeps pushing past what’s possible today. They’re adopting new tools and platforms as technology changes, and building toward AI-powered analytics and agentic systems on top of their data with AWS Quick. Figure 3: Vanessa Gonzalez, Vice President of AI at FIG, presenting Technology is changing fast, and FIG wants to be at the front of that change. Building on its existing analytics, FIG moved to AWS Quick, a platform that brings AI into its dashboards, reporting, and analytics. AWS Quick is FIG’s “single front door” for enterprise analytics. It brings together structured data such as customer relationship management (CRM) systems, databases, and finance data. It also pulls in unstructured content such as internal knowledge bases, policy documents, and collateral, through a governed data layer. That gives FIG a base for AI-powered insights and agentic workflows built on its own data. The AI analytics loop : Moving from reporting on what already happened to a continuous cycle: Ask → Analyze → Automate → Act. Centralized discovery : An analytics portal organized by business area (sales, operations, marketing, commissions), with built-in AI chat assistants so teams can talk directly to their documents and datasets. Democratized insights : Self-service exploration tools for non-technical business users, plus a learning hub that builds prompt engineering and AI skills across teams while keeping proper governance in place. Figure 4: FIG’s vision for its future with AWS Quick Hands-on: Building apps and no-code flows Attendees worked through two hands-on exercises: Build an AWS Quick app in 50 minutes : Every attendee in the room successfully designed and launched a custom application in AWS Quick. This showed how fast non-technical users and developers alike can deploy purpose-built decision tools without writing code. AWS Quick Flows workshop : A subset of six participants dove deeper into workflow automation. They built multi-step, event-triggered flows that handle repetitive data tasks, replacing manual reporting handoffs with automated, repeatable pipelines. Figure 5: The DC user group building apps together One of the key takeaways is how quickly teams can go from an idea to a working solution with AWS Quick. New ideas now take hours or even minutes to build, not weeks or months. Looking ahead and getting involved Figure 6: Attendees during the closing group discussion The event concluded with an open group discussion where attendees shared practical observations on bridging the gap between legacy infrastructure and generative AI. As organizations move toward agentic architectures, the consensus from the DC user group was clear: successful AI adoption isn’t only about selecting a foundation model. It starts with intentional data design, unified access, and empowering teams to build practical automations. Building fast isn’t only about tools. It also means learning from each other, which is why events like this matter. Next steps Ready to try it yourself? Start with the AWS Quick product page and the AWS Quick user guide , then connect a data source you already use and ask your first question. From there, try building an app or an AWS Quick Flows automation for a task your team repeats every week. Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories
items.description: The computer gaming world hasn't heard much from Will Wright ( SimCity , The Sims ) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright's subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA . Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players' memories. MyMems , which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright's previous projects by "turn[ing] the simulation inward," as Wright's Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning . The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world. “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?" Wright says by way of example in the release. "If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?" Read full article Comments

items.title: datasette-arrows 0.1a0
items.description: Release: datasette-arrows 0.1a0 Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats. I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it. Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot. Add the plugin to Datasette ( datasette install datasette-arrows ) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option: This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release. Tags: datasette , projects

items.description: The PSF end-of-year fundraiser With my Python Software Foundation board director hat on: we've launched our end-of-year fundraiser for the non-profit that supports Python development and the Python community. If your company or your work benefits from Python, please consider donating this year! The PSF looks after the IP behind Python, operates PyPI, sponsors core developer sprints, supports community events (including running PyCon US every year), and employs a small and excellent staff team to keep everything running. We also operate the Developers in Residence program , which now includes three security developers (welcome, Brett Smith) focused on helping secure Python, PyPI, and the wider ecosystem. Tags: python , psf

items.title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
items.description: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack . You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

items.title: Startup Makes Headway Towards Formalizing All of Math With AI
items.description: As Axiom Math ’s AI swarm was putting the final touches on the automatic verification of 15,000-page proof of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups (CFSG) , colloquially referred to as the ‘enormous theorem’, on Sunday 25 October, the company’s Founding Mathematician Ken Ono had nothing to do but watch and reflect on the achievement. As the son of a mathematician , he had grown up surrounded by some of the architects of the CFSG’s proof, widely considered to be the longest mathematical proof ever written by humans. Now, he was contributing to formally verifying what his father and peers had created. “My wife was with me as I watched the team countdown to completing the verification,” he recalls. “God, I cannot tell you how emotional I was.” University of St Andrews group theorist Colva Roney-Dougal (who was not involved in the work) says of formalizing CFSG: “I held it up as an example of something that was going to be incredibly hard to formalize because I had thought that the amount of computing it was going to require was just unattainable,” she says. “So when I heard the announcement, I was really, really surprised.” This result, along with the concurrent formal verification of the 7500-page Stacks project , represent a huge AI engineering achievement and lay some of the groundwork for digitizing all mathematics. Formally enormous Why the hoo-ha? The CFSG concerns finite simple groups. These are groups (sets of elements combined with an operation, like addition or multiplication, that follows specific rules) that are simple (in other words, cannot be reduced or simplified further) and finite (as opposed to groups containing an infinite number of elements). For example, all the permutations of a deck of cards form a simple finite group. Évariste Galois laid the foundations for group theory almost 200 years ago. Finite simple groups have since been classified by myriad mathematicians into 18 families (plus 26 sporadic simple groups that do not belong to any of these families). The CFSG’s proof confirms that this list is complete. But this simple task was only achieved by bringing together results and arguments that far exceed what any individual mathematician can fully absorb from more than 500 journal articles written by around 100 authors over a half-century period. Translating this interconnected web of knowledge into code and verifying its correctness therefore posed a number of significant engineering challenges, even beyond those overcome in earlier proof formalizations by Axiom Math this year . One of the hardest, according to Axiom Math’s Niels Voss , who led the CFSG formalization, was the sheer length of the proof. Over 15,000 pages of dense mathematics, the CFSG proof contains multiple theorems, lemmas, and definitions none of which can be checked until everything has been made machine-readable. To get around this required some ingenuity. “We processed all the literature from the CFSG, and traced the network structure of the informal proof before we were able to start working on it,” says Voss. “We then broke up the statement of the CFSG into about 100 milestones—landmark results along the way that can be independently verified—which we used to guide the formalization and stay on track.” Roney-Dougal says she is very impressed with the result, and particularly appreciates how the formal proof finds and clears up several mistakes in the original human proof. She thinks this result is critical to formalizing any modern research in group theory, such as her own work understanding how simple finite groups behave. But, Roney-Dougal says, because the verification was done automatically, there are few mathematicians capable of extracting information from the proof to share with the community, and that a new generation of mathematicians may have “missed a chance to gain knowledge from the doing of it”. Stacks of ingenuity required Just nine days after the CFSG formalization announcement, Axion Math revealed it had automatically formalized the Stacks project, too. Started in 2005 by Columbia University mathematician Aise Johan de Jong , Stacks is a massive, open-source collaborative mathematics textbook and reference work focused on highly abstract algebraic geometry and algebraic stacks (geometric spaces that are vital to modern string theory and number theory). Whereas CFSG is a single (huge) landmark theorem, the Stacks project is essentially a well-structured library of thousands of interlocking definitions, constructions, and lemmas bringing all of modern algebraic geometry together. The final Stacks formalization stands at a mere 16 million lines of code (compared to CFSG’s 43 million lines of code, roughly on a par with the Linux kernel), but it presented a different challenge to Axiom Math engineers: needing to achieve faithfulness and coherence across thousands of interlocking definitions and theorems, says Axiom Math’s Vasily Ilin , who led the project. This required the team to design a hierarchical system of AI agents with specialized responsibilities working in parallel, keeping every definition aligned across the library, while also checking faithfulness with multi-agent audits, cross-checks against sources, and hard tests. This ensured that every element and task aligned across the entire project. A highly efficient, general, reusable, and maintainable formal library of foundational concepts underpinning much of modern mathematics, the impact of the Stacks formalization could be profound. Now, anyone or any bot can access the formal Stacks library and build new formal mathematics upon it. And together, the CFSG and Stacks formalizations represent a significant step toward formalizing all of mathematics. “They show the two ways formalization has to scale: one very long proof, and one very wide body of connected theory,” says Ono. items.title: Will AI Coding Eat Video Game Engines?
items.description: When Travis McGeathy’s studio, Seeker Entertainment, ran out of funding in September, its game KinForge went down with it. KinForge was an online game built in Unreal Engine 5.7 and designed to run on servers hosted by Amazon Web Services (AWS). With no one left to pay the server bill, the game became unplayable even for those few developers, including studio co-founder McGeathy, who had the code. Then, on a whim, McGeathy pointed Anthropic’s Claude Code at the project and asked it to make KinForge playable without AWS. After four hours of mostly hands-off work he had a build that let players host their own games. Claude added support for peer-to-peer play over both the Internet and a local area network. To McGeathy’s surprise, it also added persistent save states, a feature that lets players resume a game if they’re disconnected. Although KinForge is still built in Unreal Engine, developments like this could give companies that create game engines cause for concern. The conversion was accomplished with an agentic AI workflow that partially bypasses the elaborate, user-friendly game engine UI that many companies, including Unreal Engine creator Epic Games, have spent decades perfecting. Anthropic’s Fable 5.2, released November 9, further upped the ante. The model is capable of generating a 3D game with a custom game engine in the style of the hit Call of Duty series. This raises a question: can game engines evolve quickly enough to keep pace with model improvements? “We’re definitely in a world where I can just dream up software really fast. So, if Unreal Engine was static, what’s the value at the end of next year? This is why we are pivoting hard towards velocity,” says Daniel Vogel , chief operating officer at Epic Games. “I think with any fixed set of features or functionality, it can eventually be replicated. If we’re doing our job right, we’re pushing the engine and pushing the envelope forward.” From Code to Nodes, and Back Again Major game engines often offer developers new visual tools and workflows that help them build games while interacting with less code. Unreal Engine’s Blueprints, a graphically based system introduced in Unreal Engine 4 that lets designers script gameplay simply by wiring boxes together, is an example. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , an award-winning game from French studio Sandfall Interactive, leaned heavily on Blueprints for scripting gameplay encounters . That should have been proof of the feature’s success. Instead, Epic will remove Blueprints in Unreal Engine 6 (UE6). Why? Blame LLMs. “AI doesn’t handle Blueprints very well,” says McGeathy. “It would much rather work with the code.” Currently, LLMs interact with Unreal Engine primarily through a Model Context Protocol server . MCP is an open-source standard created by Anthropic that lets AI send commands to software. “It’s not actually moving the mouse,” says Ryan Barker , a gameplay and systems engineer who has worked on projects for Amazon Games and Sony Online Entertainment. “It’s sending signals to the editor that the editor understands.” UE6 will lean into that reality by moving all code to Verse, a text-based programming language that will replace both Blueprints and Unreal Engine 5’s C++ gameplay framework. UE6 will also replace Unreal’s actor framework, which is based on object-oriented programming , with Scene Graph, which resembles an entity component system . “Typically, an ECS is a lot harder to code around,” says Barker, but ECS can provide superior game performance and result in less duplicate code . An LLM can help manage the complexity. Verse debuted in Unreal Editor for Fortnite in 2023, while Scene Graph arrived in 2024. Verse was designed to let millions of creators run code side by side in Fortnite, so it’s strict. The compiler catches mistakes before code runs and limits what each function can do. And because Scene Graph is built on Verse, an AI can work with a game world through code. That’s different from Blueprints, which are stored as binary files that LLMs can’t read directly. In addition to these changes, UE6 will make the engine more modular and expose its systems through an application programming interface “so that AI tooling can get at them without needing to fall back to slow computer use,” says Marcus Wassmer , the executive vice president of development at Epic Games. An internal effort that Epic calls “Python All The Things” aims to make everything in the editor scriptable. UE6 will also store more game assets as text so an LLM can edit them directly. For binary assets (non-text files) that remain, Epic is building a command-line tool that allows agents to interact with the files without loading the full UE6 interface. The traditional Unreal Engine editor isn’t going away, but Vogel expects it will change as LLM use becomes more common. “You’re not going to move stuff visually in the editor. Those times are gone,” he says. Instead, he expects game developers will more frequently use the Unreal Engine editor to visualize “the context needed to make decisions, or make the tweaks.” Unreal Engine 5.9 offers a glimpse at what that transition will mean in practice. Released as a developer preview on 9 November , it includes a new feature called Unreal Canvas . Vogel says it’s a collaboration feature that takes inspiration from visual workspace software like Miro . “It’s a way to make sense of the project,” says Vogel. Why Buy an Engine When You Can Build One? Epic Games’ goal is to keep Unreal Engine relevant in a world where AI coding tools are becoming ever-more capable. The company has the benefit of approaching the problem from a position of strength : Unreal Engine is the second most commonly used engine, after Unity Technologies’ Unity engine, and ranks first if measured by the number of games sold. Will that be enough? McGeathy says there can be benefits to creating an engine from scratch. “If you own the engine, you’re not reliant on a third party who could yank it o

items.title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
items.description: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases. Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science. OSMO AI A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary. Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.) The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later. Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes. But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows , has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack , arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication. Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since. But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. items.title: Neural Classifiers as Error-Correcting Codes
items.description: arXiv:2611.18239v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A unified framework is proposed that characterizes supervised deep classification as the decoding of error-correcting codes in the Shannon sense. Cross-entropy optimization is shown to align softmax classifiers with maximum-likelihood decoding, where logits map to Hamming distances to class-specific codewords. This correspondence explains the emergence of standard divergence objectives (e.g., Kullback-Leibler, Jeffreys, Bregman) and provides a geometric basis for the stability of decision boundaries. Furthermore, the geometries of Neural Collapse and LeJEPA are identified as optimal constellations for decoding under isotropic noise. Unlike classical Error-Correcting Output Codes, deep networks are shown to learn effective codebooks in the feature space implicitly. This insight is leveraged to derive novel criteria for lossless quantization, improved knowledge distillation, and architectural regularization based on code redundancy. Finally, this perspective is extended to self-supervised encoders, offering a cohesive explanation for the geometry of latent representations in modern neural models.

items.title: Asymptotic Margins and Feature Confinement in Conic Classification Heads under Softmax Cross-Entropy
items.description: arXiv:2611.18507v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Classification heads built on conic functions give each class a bounded region of the feature space, and such regions are used to reject samples of unseen classes. We ask whether these regions also keep the features bounded when the head is trained with softmax cross-entropy. For a head whose class scores combine a linear term with a Euclidean norm, we first show that the region of each class is bounded by a quadric of revolution, whose eccentricity is the reciprocal of one learned ratio. We then attach to each class an asymptotic margin, which compares the growth of its score with the growth of all the other scores and can be computed by a second-order cone program. The loss of a class has infimum zero exactly when its margin is positive, and it then approaches zero only along diverging features. When the margin is negative, the loss is coercive and its minimizers lie in an explicit ball. Since softmax depends only on the differences between scores, a class with a bounded region can still have a positive margin, so bounded regions do not confine the features. The result extends to other norms, including the polyhedral conic functions. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, all 1210 cells of 67 trained conic heads have positive margins, whereas a prototype head keeps nine of its ten cells bounded, as the theory predicts.

items.title: Score-based neural ordinary differential equations for reaction-diffusions
items.description: arXiv:2611.18467v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A diffusion equation can be rewritten as a transport equation driven by the score function of the evolving density. Conventional probability-flow formulations, which move particles deterministically with this score-driven velocity, typically conserve total mass. In this work, we develop a Lagrangian method for reaction-diffusion equations in which each particle carries a position and a physical weight. The characteristic ODEs incorporate source terms into the evolution of the log-density and its gradient, while particle weights track changes in mass. We combine this representation with a learned velocity field and weighted particle training to approximate these dynamics. For non-increasing reaction rates, a relative-entropy inequality supports the mass-normalized self-consistency residual as the training objective. This objective can control the error of the induced density when the growth rate is bounded. The algorithm divides the time interval into short windows. In each window, a frozen velocity generates the particle data for a regression of the network velocity. We draw the particles from period-adapted initial sampling distributions and weight them in the loss partly by their predicted future mass, because the reaction can make regions with little initial mass important later. We numerically investigate the method on the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) equation with a linear source term, Fisher-KPP equations, and Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao gradient flows.

items.title: Interpret Policies in Deep Reinforcement Learning using SILVER with RL-Guided Labeling: A Model-level Approach to High-dimensional and Multi-action Environments
items.description: arXiv:2510.19244v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) achieves remarkable performance but lacks interpretability, limiting trust in policy behavior. The existing SILVER framework (Li, Siddique, and Cao 2025) explains RL policy via Shapley-based regression but remains restricted to low-dimensional, binary-action domains. We propose SILVER with RL-guided labeling, an enhanced variant that extends SILVER to multi-action and high-dimensional environments by incorporating the RL policy's own action outputs into the boundary points identification. Our method first extracts compact feature representations from image observations, performs SHAP-based feature attribution, and then employs RL-guided labeling to generate behaviorally consistent boundary datasets. Surrogate models, such as decision trees and regression-based functions, are subsequently trained to interpret RL policy's decision structure. We evaluate the proposed framework on two Atari environments using three deep RL algorithms and conduct human-subject study to assess the clarity and trustworthiness of the derived interpretable policy. Results show that our approach maintains competitive task performance while substantially improving transparency and human understanding of agent behavior. This work advances explainable RL by transforming SILVER into a scalable and behavior-aware framework for interpreting deep RL agents in high-dimensional, multi-action settings.

items.title: LEGIT: Live Eligibility Gating over Identifier Tries for Constrained Decoding of Heterogeneous Pages
items.description: arXiv:2611.10357v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A generative recommender names each candidate with a short token sequence, a Semantic ID, and recommends by generating those tokens. Some generative recommenders, including the Uber Eats search engine we are building, write a whole results page, stores with their menu items, in one decoding pass. Every Semantic ID on such a page must name a real store or item that is eligible for the search, such as a store that delivers to the user's location, and that is not already on the page. Each item must also belong to the store above it. A trie over the catalog keeps identifiers real, but eligibility and repetition change with every request and token, and the grammar-constrained decoder we tried could not enforce these changing rules exactly and quickly. We call this constraint LEGIT, for live eligibility gating over identifier tries. Numbering trie leaves depth first turns each rule into a range lookup over one store trie and one item trie, and every generated page passes an independent catalog check. On one NVIDIA B200 GPU with one or two requests per decode step, a direct implementation that walks the trie on the GPU makes each token about 5 times as slow as unconstrained decoding. Across 36 implementations, hardware counters and ablations are consistent with kernel launches and CPU-GPU waits as the source of this slowdown. Our fastest implementation walks the trie on the CPU while the GPU runs the model, needs no custom kernel, and cuts time per output token by 65.9 percent against the direct GPU implementation, to about 1.7 times the unconstrained cost. This implementation is also the fastest on a page layout that puts each item before its store.

items.title: Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
items.description: arXiv:2611.21799v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations. Our code can be found on https://github.com/yongzx/cot-control-model-organism.

items.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
items.description: arXiv:2611.21885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.

items.title: On Formal Counterfactual Explanations
items.description: arXiv:2611.22010v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.

items.title: MedGuardBench: A Patient-Oriented Benchmark for Personalized Guardrail Development
items.description: arXiv:2611.22069v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Safety is personal: the same action can be safe for one person but unsafe for another. Yet current guardrails judge content without considering who is affected. Using medication safety, we introduce \textit{patient-conditioned medication guarding}, which predicts a safety verdict and 17 risk categories from a patient profile and prescription. We release \textbf{MedGuardBench}, a drug-disjoint benchmark of 5{,}001 scenarios across 87 medications. We find that standard guardrails rely on surface cues, such as wording and profile presence, rather than patient facts. To address this, we develop \textit{personalized reasoning guardrails} with three components. \textbf{Personalized Reasoning Distillation} links risks to relevant patient fields. \textbf{Context Unrolling (CU)} makes models check each field themselves, reducing false alarms on most backbones; controls show that providing the check does not yield the same benefit. A \textbf{rule-based reward (guided GRPO)} improves unsafe recall and complex-risk detection, including allergies and adverse reactions, on some backbones, but increases false alarms on others. Our models outperform base models and matched no-profile controls in accuracy, while reducing false alarms relative to no-profile controls. Profile removal and swapping confirm that gains come from patient information, not fine-tuning alone.

items.title: LoCaR: Localized Canvas Retrieval With Frozen Vision-Language Model
items.description: arXiv:2611.22131v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Whole image embeddings can under represent small objects and local attributes that distinguish relevant images for localized queries. We present LoCaR, a training free framework for localized text to image retrieval with frozen vision language models. LoCaR constructs and utilizes independent proposals (SAM2) focusing on the object so as to get a more localized representation that independently encodes each region using the frozen visual encoder. We further study paired-support adaptation as an optional residual that uses matched text region exemplars without updating the underlying encoders. We also introduce LOCFG, a Visual Genome derived benchmark designed to evaluate localized retrieval for smaller and more challenging referents. Across several vision language backbones, our results show that improving the region representation itself is the main source of gain.

items.title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents
items.description: arXiv:2611.22288v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. An adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485. We report an attack class the projection misses.

items.title: Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning
items.description: arXiv:2611.22330v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply-demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector-Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.

items.title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.22456v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.

items.title: PACT: Plan-Action Consistency Training by Preserving Correct Plans and Repairing Actions in GUI Agents
items.description: arXiv:2611.22591v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GUI agents can formulate a correct immediate plan in their reasoning yet emit an action that fails to execute it, creating an execution gap. This recurring mismatch undermines reliable task completion, as a single execution error can derail a multi-step workflow. In outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, broadcasting a negative response-level advantage across all generated tokens risks penalizing valid planning together with erroneous execution. To address this credit-assignment conflict, we introduce PACT (Plan-Action Consistency Training), a training framework that combines reference-aligned plan protection and plan-aligned action repair without altering the original scalar action reward. Using annotated reference actions to identify execution gaps, PACT protects the verified plan by masking negative policy-gradient contributions across its token span. Keeping the generated reasoning unchanged as context, it then favors the reference action over the emitted erroneous action through a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights. Compared with the outcome-only baseline, PACT raises AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), while improving rule-based plan-action consistency on AndroidControl High from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp). Adapting PACT to desktop agents also improves task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp) on the full 369-task OSWorld benchmark. Together, these results establish PACT as an effective credit-assignment framework for bridging execution gaps and improving task completion across mobile and desktop GUI environments.

items.title: COTTI: Contrastive Training and Time-Aware Inference for Robust Industrial Recommendation under Promotional Drift
items.description: arXiv:2611.22597v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Promotional events shift traffic composition, purchase behavior, and the scale of conversion probabilities on different time horizons. We present \textbf{COTTI} (\textbf{CO}ntrastive \textbf{T}raining and \textbf{T}ime-aware \textbf{I}nference), an industrial recommendation framework that separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment. Cross-Period Contrastive Alignment (CPC) regularizes paired histories of the same user with adaptive consistency weights. Active Re-weighting (RW) controls the influence of promotional examples through historical-interest distance. Adaptive Boundary Alignment (ABA) combines stochastic prediction variability with a temporal event kernel to adjust logits while keeping predictor parameters fixed. We analyze the weighted objective and bound ABA-induced probability and ranking changes. On Fliggy data, COTTI attains an offline AUC of 0.8127, compared with 0.8101 for TEN and 0.8123 for TEN with ABA. Cross-category analysis reveals improved discrimination alongside declines in paid-item recall for novel categories. End-to-end measurements give a p99 latency of 38.9\,ms and throughput of 14,700 requests/s; enabling ABA adds 2.2\,ms to p99. A ten-day online experiment against the serving HDR model yields relative gains of 3.14\% in conversion rate and 2.68\% in revenue per mille. Together, these results characterize the trade-off between aggregate prediction, novel-category discovery, and serving cost in promotional recommendation.

items.title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
items.description: arXiv:2611.22248v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{OAK-Mind}, a zer\textbf{O}-training, multi-\textbf{A}gent, \textbf{K}nowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

items.title: AI Simulations Grounded in Rich Self-Reports Increase Accuracy and Reduce Distortion
items.description: arXiv:2411.10109v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI simulations of people built from demographic prompts often misjudge individuals and distort sample-level patterns. We test whether rich self-report data reduce these problems. We developed an AI voice interviewer and conducted two-hour interviews following the American Voices Project protocol with 1,052 U.S. adults, who also completed surveys and behavioral experiments. For each participant, we compared simulations prompted with demographic attributes, self-authored personas, survey responses, interview responses, or combined surveys and interviews. We evaluated accuracy on held-out responses, and measured eight statistical distortions at the sample level: biased averages, compressed variance, distorted response distributions, over-correlated items, attitudes collapsing onto one dimension, ideological sorting, amplified experimental effects, and hyper-rationality. On General Social Survey (GSS) items, demographic simulation led to 60.4% accuracy, whereas interview and survey simulation achieved 69.4% and 69.3%, and combining them reached 72.8%, compared with 79.5% for participants' two-week test-retest agreement. Surveys and interviews also improved prediction of personality traits, but not of incentivized economic choices. Combined interview and survey simulation closed a median of 53.5% of the eight distortion gaps between demographic simulation and participant responses. An open-weight model fine-tuned on other participants' self-reports and responses to the target questions achieved 75.2% GSS accuracy and closed a median of 69.3% of the distortion gap. Overall, both frontier and fine-tuned models reduced distortions without erasing them, but neither reduced hyper-rationality in economic games. These findings demonstrate that qualitative and quantitative self-reports can improve person-specific simulations and reduce statistical distortions.

items.title: Toward AI epidemiology: a measurement standardization framework for prospective risk detection
items.description: arXiv:2512.15783v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper proposes a measurement standardization framework that compresses expert-AI interactions into structured, comparable fields for prospective risk detection in deployed AI systems, without access to model internals. This concept paper defines the framework's scope, semantically and statistically, and specifies a protocol for its empirical testing. The population-level claims it is designed to support therefore belong to a staged research program rather than to results claimed here. Measurement standardization underpins three claims. The first is a reliability claim: under bounded conditions, large language models can produce reliable, standardized assessments of the evidential and policy alignment of expert-AI interactions. The second is a governance claim: alignment scores give experts an immediate signal during deployment and give institutions a basis for monitoring alignment patterns across mission types, models, and domains. The third is an outcome validation claim: once measurement standardization is established, aggregate alignment scores could be used to study associations with downstream outcomes in regulated professional settings. This introduces the possibility of an "AI epidemiology", a form of risk detection based on correlated variables instead of mechanistic analysis, inspired by epidemiological reasoning. A minimal application of the protocol to a published expert-AI corpus shows that the judge reproduces its policy and evidential alignment scores across two runs under the specified conditions. Judge reliability at scale remains to be validated in future work. The paper sets out a defined grammar of eight interaction fields, together with a statistical protocol based on paired bootstrap inference, DeLong's test for paired AUCs as a sensitivity check, a pre-specified one-sided non-inferiority margin of 0.05, and Holm-Bonferroni correction.

items.title: CORE: Concept-Oriented Reinforcement for Bridging the Definition-Application Gap in Mathematical Reasoning
items.description: arXiv:2512.18857v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often solve challenging math exercises yet fail to apply the concept right when the problem requires genuine understanding. Popular Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) pipelines reinforce final answers but provide little fine-grained conceptual signal, so models improve at pattern reuse rather than conceptual applications. We introduce CORE (Concept-Oriented REinforcement), an RL training framework that turns explicit concepts into a controllable supervision signal. Starting from a high-quality, low-contamination textbook resource that links verifiable exercises to concise concept descriptions, we run a sanity probe showing LLMs can restate definitions but fail concept-linked quizzes, quantifying the conceptual reasoning gap. CORE then (i) synthesizes concept-aligned quizzes, (ii) injects brief concept snippets during rollouts to elicit concept-primed trajectories, and (iii) reinforces conceptual reasoning via trajectory replacement after group failures, a lightweight forward-KL constraint that aligns unguided with concept-primed policies, or standard GRPO directly on concept-aligned quizzes. Across several models, CORE delivers consistent gains over vanilla and SFT baselines on both in-domain concept-exercise suites and diverse out-of-domain math benchmarks. CORE unifies direct training on concept-aligned quizzes and concept-injected rollouts under outcome regularization. It provides fine-grained conceptual supervision that bridges problem-solving competence and genuine conceptual reasoning, while remaining algorithm- and verifier-agnostic.

items.title: CardioLoom: A Report-Guided Electrocardiogram Foundation Model for Cross-Domain Cardiovascular Phenotyping
items.description: arXiv:2605.25446v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Routine electrocardiogram (ECG) reports offer scalable supervision for cardiovascular representation learning. In this retrospective study, we pretrained CardioLoom, a report-guided ECG foundation model, on 2,781,289 ECG-report pairs from 1,298,359 patients. Downstream development used a separate cohort of 721,317 ECGs from 233,798 patients. Evaluation covered 89 targets, with external testing in nine cohorts. Across 45 internal ECG diagnoses, macro area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) was 0.624 versus 0.615 for DeepECG-SSL. Across 203 external ECG evaluations, corresponding means were 0.425 and 0.424. Using labels from 10% of training patients, CardioLoom achieved macro-AUPRC 0.559, exceeding supervised training with all labels (0.549). For heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, AUPRCs were 0.690, 0.641 and 0.677 in Zhongshan, Shiyuan and BIDMC. Cardiac amyloidosis screening yielded 4.5% positive predictive value using a threshold targeting 99% specificity in validation. Report-guided pretraining supported label-efficient ECG diagnosis, with variable transfer across echocardiographic phenotypes.

items.title: Latent Goal Prediction from Language for Model-Based Planning
items.description: arXiv:2606.20627v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) enable agents to plan in latent space by imagining the outcomes of candidate actions, yet task specification remains a bottleneck. Visual targets provide precise local gradients but poor distant guidance, while language is flexible yet limited by noisy cross-modal alignment or dependence on distinct large generative models. We introduce LAGO (Latent Goal Prediction from Language), a hierarchical world model in which a single predictor both forecasts action-conditioned dynamics and grounds language instructions as sequences of intermediate latent subgoals, training both modes with a single regression objective over a shared latent space. At each planning step, LAGO predicts a sequence of latent subgoals from a language instruction and optimizes an action sequence using a soft-minimum alignment cost that rewards subgoal proximity without enforcing a rigid path. Subgoals are repredicted as the agent's state evolves, turning a single long-horizon instruction into a sequence of locally tractable objectives. Across environments spanning navigation and manipulation, LAGO outperforms flat and hierarchical image-goal planners, with the largest gains on long-horizon navigation with curved, hazard-constrained paths, where it more than doubles the success rate of a goal-conditioned behavior cloning policy trained on the same demonstrations. Grounding language in the world model's own latent space also outperforms vision-language reward models, including one that plans with ground-truth dynamics.

items.title: Test-Time Coverage: Test-Conditioned Data Curation for Deployment-Aware Learning
items.description: arXiv:2607.22697v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deployed AI systems are often trained from broad candidate data pools, necessitating data curation towards the deployment test distribution. However, standard data curation methods score training-side criteria rather than directly optimizing deployment match. We introduce TTCov (Test-Time Coverage), a data-level test-conditioned curation method that uses test-side information before training instead of updating model weights at inference. TTCov decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution. To represent coverage, it builds a task Atlas, a collection of LLM-based atomic propositions (APs) describing deployment-relevant concepts, seeded from open task knowledge and expanded with unmatched APs extracted from unlabeled deployment samples. To represent distribution, it instantiates the matched deployment APs with their frequencies, yielding a Knowledge Atlas (K-Atlas) that operationalizes the deployment distribution as a curation target. TTCov then selects a budgeted training set whose deployment APs distribution approximates this target. We apply TTCov towards autonomous driving (AD), keeping adaptation off the inference path while selecting data with greater deployment-relevant coverage, closer K-Atlas matching, and stronger downstream end-to-end driving performance than data-curation baselines, including seamless adaptability to novel domains via city-to-city expansion. Code available at https://github.com/NVlabs/TTCov.

items.title: Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration
items.description: arXiv:2611.19345v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a recurrent model is replaced, its old state may not determine what the new model would compute from the same history. We characterize the information that must be retained before the replacement is known. For a time-invariant affine linear family, the minimum continuous causal memory for order-$k$ local migration equals the reachable dimension of a lifted coefficient system minus the information in the anchor state. A controllable $d$-state model with scalar input needs at most $kd$ additional real coordinates, even when arbitrary matrix replacement directions are revealed only after streaming. A single rank-one direction can already require all $kd$. Conditional singular values and auxiliary-bit bounds distinguish this local information law from recovery at a fixed tolerance. We also give invariant-subspace and future-output constructions. Controlled experiments compare the resulting representations. In a small language model, equal-memory cubic interpolation improves mean state fidelity over third-order coefficients but provides no meaningful predictive gain. An analytic history basis preserves useful adaptation more economically in a coupled identification task. With repeated slow poles, eight history coordinates meet normalized output error $10^{-4}$ across five fitted seeds despite substantial full-state error. Splitting the poles raises the smallest tested successful width to 64.

items.title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
items.description: arXiv:2611.20794v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide semantic features for uplift estimation, but treatment-revealing text can induce prediction shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose \emph{LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization} (\textsc{LULR}) to address this risk. With the LLM encoder frozen, \textsc{LULR} penalizes dependence between the causal head's trainable shared representation and treatment while retaining separate outcome heads. The penalty uses a variational approximation to the contrastive log-ratio upper bound (CLUB) of mutual information, targeting treatment dependence rather than generic parameter shrinkage. Controlled proxy experiments provide exploratory evidence of improved ranking scores under injected treatment information relative to no regularization and the tested weight-decay setting. Structured-only benchmarks show modest, dataset-dependent effects. On an industrial pricing randomized controlled trial, mean offline $\text{lift@}0.3$ is $0.258$ for \textsc{LULR}, compared with $0.106$ for the same-backbone baseline. A separate one-week online A/B test of the complete deployed pricing policy records $5.45\%$ higher sales volume and $1.91\%$ higher gross merchandise value than the control arm. These short-term policy-level gains do not isolate the regularizer's effect.

items.title: Limite 1B - Violetto: Technical Report
items.description: arXiv:2611.21646v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present Limite 1B - Violetto, a one-billion-parameter model designed for high-throughput mathematical reasoning. Limite is trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a carefully curated, mathematics-centric corpus and supports context lengths of up to 131k tokens. Its architecture and training recipe were developed together to maximize reasoning capability while keeping training and inference costs low. Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum. Limite achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, placing it among models many times its size on our evaluation suite. The model is deliberately only lightly instruction-tuned: it is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver and as a fast, parallel component of larger systems, rather than as a general-purpose assistant. We release the model, its base and value checkpoints, and an optimized serving implementation under the Apache 2.0 license.

items.title: Latent Fact Composition under Next-Token Training
items.description: arXiv:2611.21921v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Controlled studies of latent two-hop reasoning train transformers to predict only the answer, whereas language models are trained to predict every token. We ask whether a model trained on every token learns to answer two-hop questions whose intermediate entity appears in no two-hop training example. We build a synthetic corpus with such questions. On this corpus every term of the loss can be computed exactly. A looped transformer, a standard transformer and DiscoLoop answer almost none of these questions. We therefore introduce the Baton family of looped transformers. They pass the intermediate entity to the second loop as a token embedding. When trained to predict only the answer, two of its three variants answer these questions almost perfectly. We then relate the success and failure of each model to three design conditions. Experiments that change one condition at a time agree with this hypothesis. When Baton is trained on every token, however, its accuracy on these questions rises and then declines. We further split the gradient of the next-token loss into three terms. Removing the two terms that depend on the particular training set raises the peak accuracy but does not remove the decline. The decline arises in the second hop while the model still recalls both facts.

items.title: What MoE Routing Controls: Causal Interventions on Expert Trajectories
items.description: arXiv:2611.22120v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, a token is routed to a sequence of experts across layers. We investigate how forcing tokens onto chosen expert paths influences model behavior. We build a target path from the experts that a concept's or role's tokens most often use, and we add a fixed bias to each target expert's router logit during generation to steer the token toward this expert path. We study two kinds of targets. Format targets concern the form of the output, and concept targets concern its topic. In Qwen3-30B-A3B, we show that steering a format path changes the text the model writes. We also show that steering a concept path shifts the model's next-token probabilities toward the concept, even when the path is built in another language, yet this shift has little effect on the generated text. We investigate why formats reach the text but concepts do not by steering only part of the generation, and find evidence that a format, once started, reinforces itself. We show that the concepts religion and money steer most strongly, and that the effect is concentrated in the middle layers. We attempt to explain why the strength of the effect varies by concept through an analysis of embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.

items.title: RISA: Recoverable Sparse Attention for Block-Diffusion Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.22191v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Block-wise diffusion language models (DLMs) refine multiple tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. Their long-context inference, however, remains bottlenecked by memory-bound attention: every denoising step repeatedly reads a growing historical key--value (KV) cache. Directly applying sparse attention does not fully solve this problem, because different queries can select different pages, inflating the block's collective read set, while repeated support construction adds overhead and permanent eviction can discard information needed later. We present RISA, a recoverable sparse-attention method with shared read plans for block-wise DLMs. RISA exploits the fact that historical KV remains fixed within a block while queries evolve across denoising steps. Newly generated history is organized into exact priority and recovery tiers; seed queries then build a protected, bounded read plan whose indices are reused across the block while attention is recomputed with fresh queries and current-block KV. This separates history preservation from repeated reading and amortizes sparse-support construction without changing the backbone or decoder. On DreamReasoner-8B, RISA retains comparable task performance. At 32K, the default configuration speeds up attention by $2.67\times$ and fixed-trajectory requests by $1.36\times$ over dense, and attention speedup reaches $5.53\times$ at 128K. Across eight settings on three models, RISA decodes faster than the tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.

items.title: Zero-Dimensional Attention Topology for Linguistic Acceptability
items.description: arXiv:2611.22312v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Topological summaries of Transformer attention provide sentence representations for linguistic acceptability classification. We examine a zero-dimensional persistent-homology ($H_0$) representation that summarizes minimum-spanning-tree merge values from 144 symmetrized BERT attention graphs into 1,440 features. The retrospective evaluation uses 8,517 downstream training sentences and 521 in-domain and 497 out-of-domain CoLA validation sentences after data-integrity filtering. The recorded out-of-domain Matthews correlation coefficients are 0.438 for the topological representation and 0.508 for attention statistics, compared with 0.545 for BERT. Attention-feature results are retained aggregate measurements; BERT predictions are rescored and length controls are refitted from the accompanying records. Analytical results show that the representation retains token-count information and discards a class of directional attention differences. Source resampling of BERT predictions also demonstrates the sensitivity of uncertainty estimates to the sampling unit. The reported results do not demonstrate a predictive advantage for this fixed topological representation over simpler attention summaries. They identify representation properties and evaluation controls relevant to subsequent studies of attention topology.

items.title: Clustering in pure-attention hardmax transformers and its role in sentiment analysis
items.description: arXiv:2407.01602v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transformers are extremely successful machine learning models whose mathematical properties remain poorly understood. Here, we rigorously characterize the behavior of transformers with hardmax self-attention and normalization sublayers as the number of layers tends to infinity. By viewing such transformers as discrete-time dynamical systems describing the evolution of points in a Euclidean space, and thanks to a geometric interpretation of the self-attention mechanism based on hyperplane separation, we show that the transformer inputs asymptotically converge to a clustered equilibrium determined by special points called \textit{leaders}. We then leverage this theoretical understanding to solve sentiment analysis problems from language processing using a fully interpretable transformer model, which effectively captures `context' by clustering meaningless words around leader words carrying the most meaning. Finally, we outline remaining challenges to bridge the gap between the mathematical analysis of transformers and their real-life implementation.

items.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
items.description: arXiv:2610.26825v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano, MemT-1.0-Flash, and MemT-1.0-Pro, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

items.title: DeltaHarness: Self-Evolving Harnesses for Resource-Adaptive Tool Execution
items.description: arXiv:2611.21688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using agents rely on execution harnesses to organize and schedule tool operations. The same task and resource description can conceal runtime conditions that reverse the latency ordering of valid execution plans. Resolving this uncertainty requires firsthand execution in the target setting. We introduce DeltaHarness, an execution-guided policy-search method that adapts agent harnesses from cold-start measurements. Its QHI loop uses the observed response to update runtime dispatch, revise physical plans, and select experiments for later proposals. An independent confirmation panel controls policy replacement. With fixed dispatch, a revised materialization policy reduces complete-delivery latency by 30.0% on one video-editing task across three fresh pairs. On held-out tasks, the evolved policies reduce latency by 8.2% relative to the best fixed plan in one seed and by 4.6% relative to the initial proposal in another.

items.title: Layerwise Learning-Rate Scaling in Vision Networks: Effective-Rate Identification, Power-Mean Aggregation, and Budget Dependence
items.description: arXiv:2611.21696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Layerwise learning-rate scaling assigns different learning rates to different parts of a network.
