Concretely, RelPrism first constructs intrinsic, relational, and hybrid attributes from distinct perspectives. It then applies multi-granularity clustering to each attribute perspective to form corresponding pseudo-task pools. Pre-training over these task pools exposes representations to comprehensive attribute perspectives and granularity levels, providing a stronger basis for downstream adaptation. Extensive experiments on 14 tasks across 5 real-world datasets show that RelPrism improves ROC-AUC by 4.15% on classification tasks and reduces MAE by 10.75% on regression tasks over state-of-the-art baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/RelPrism.

items.title: An Open-Source Training Dataset for Foundation Models for Hyperparameter Optimization
items.description: arXiv:2605.23417v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Most hyperparameter optimization methods require extensive tuning of their own hyperparameters, often limiting their ability to generalize across different benchmark families. Foundation models for hyperparameter optimization that learn optimization principles from a large collection of optimization trajectories offer a promising alternative, with the potential to outperform manually designed methods across diverse problem classes. However, prior work as either relied on non-public datasets or on purely synthetic data, limiting reproducibility and generalization to real-world problems. As a result, progress in this area has been constrained by the lack of large-scale, real-world, publicly available pre-training data. We introduce BBO-Pile, the first open-source dataset comprising over 500K optimization trajectories evaluated across 3,095 different hyperparameter optimization tasks and global optimization problems for different optimizers, which represents by far the largest public dataset for this task. Using this dataset, we train a family of foundation models at multiple scales, ranging from 2M to 80M parameters and from 200M to 2B training tokens, and study their scaling behavior with respect to compute. Our results demonstrate that large-scale pre-training is a viable and effective approach to imitate hyperparameter optimization methods, paving the way for future research in this direction.

items.title: Supervised Training Rapidly Degrades Early Visual Cortex Alignment Across Biologically Plausible Learning Rules
items.description: arXiv:2605.30556v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: CORRECTION (August 2026): the central finding of this paper is not supported. An evaluation-mode defect left the batch-normalisation layers of the predictive-coding and STDP conditions in training mode during feature extraction, producing their apparent preservation of V1 alignment. With the defect repaired, predictive coding degrades V1 alignment more than backpropagation does, not less. The finding that training degrades V1 alignment for every rule tested does survive. [Revision note: not robust to the analysis choices examined in arXiv:2611.15533.] See the correction note on page 1; the original abstract below and the body are unchanged from v1. Corrected analysis: arXiv:2608.12408. Revision note: see Comments. Random, untrained neural networks consistently match or exceed trained networks in representational similarity to early visual cortex. This puzzling finding challenges the assumption that learning improves brain alignment. We investigate it by tracking representational similarity analysis (RSA) alignment to human fMRI data across training for four learning rules: backpropagation (BP), feedback alignment (FA), predictive coding (PC), and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Using 720 object images from the THINGS database and fMRI data from three subjects across six visual ROIs, we measure Spearman correlations between model and brain representational dissimilarity matrices at eight training checkpoints (epochs 0-40). We find that (1) a single epoch of training reduces V1 alignment by 25-90%, depending on the learning rule; (2) backpropagation reduces V1 alignment most severely (delta r = -0.080), while predictive coding and STDP preserve substantially more (delta r ~ -0.04); and (3) a weaker, opposite tendency appears in object-selective cortex (LOC), where BP shows the largest increase in alignment during training, although the absolute change is small.

items.title: Multivariate Distributional Reinforcement Learning Using Sliced Divergences
items.description: arXiv:2605.31222v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) models the full return distribution rather than expectations, but extending it to multivariate settings remains challenging. Many common metrics do not naturally generalize beyond one dimension or lose computational tractability, and the multivariate case introduces additional difficulties such as general matrix discounting, for which no contraction results are available. We introduce Sliced Distributional Reinforcement Learning (SDRL), which lifts tractable one-dimensional divergences to multivariate return distributions via projections. We prove Bellman contraction for uniform slicing under shared scalar discounting, and introduce a maximum-slicing variant with contraction under general dense discount matrices. SDRL supports a broad class of base divergences; we analyze Wasserstein, Cram\'er, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), and characterize which SDRL variants suit the standard single-sample Bellman update used in distributional RL. We evaluate SDRL on a toy chain problem and a gridworld image-based environment as well as a subset of Atari games.

items.title: Semi-Supervised Learning with Noisy Proxy Covariates: Generalization Bounds and Distribution Regression
items.description: arXiv:2606.00512v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In many modern machine learning pipelines, abundant pretrained representations serve as noisy proxy covariates, while task-specific labels remain scarce. We study semi-supervised regression in this setting, and propose a simple two stage estimator that learns kernel eigenfeatures from all proxy covariates and fits a ridge predictor on labeled data. We derive finite sample bounds showing that fast labeled sample rates are recovered when proxy perturbation is controlled and unlabeled proxy covariates are sufficiently abundant. We also show that distribution regression is a direct special case, with analogous guarantees when the finite bag size is large enough. Experiments show consistent gains over supervised and semi-supervised baselines, especially in low label regimes.

items.title: Stein Kernelized Molecular Dynamics for Active Learning of Interatomic Potentials
items.description: arXiv:2606.04100v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) enable efficient and accurate atomistic simulations but depend critically on the quality and diversity of the training data. We introduce Stein kernelized molecular dynamics (SKMD), an enhanced sampling method that uses interacting particle dynamics to acquire informative training configurations for the fine-tuning of MLIPs. SKMD corresponds to a stochastic variant of Stein variational gradient descent that is adapted for molecular dynamics by incorporating asynchronous particle updates and a kernel of global atomic descriptors, which provides a symmetry-aware measure of configurational similarity. Unlike other enhanced samplers used in molecular dynamics, SKMD maintains the Boltzmann distribution as a stationary distribution of its dynamics in the appropriate asymptotic limit. This property enforces a balance between the exploration of diverse configurations and attraction toward high-probability regions of the energy landscape. We further propose an approach to efficient online data acquisition using an adaptive stopping criterion that selects non-redundant training data over the course of simulation. We demonstrate SKMD for the active learning of a neural network model of the M\"uller--Brown potential, a MACE interatomic potential for alanine dipeptide, and a MACE foundation model with a DFT oracle for predicting the Pandey reconstruction of the Si(111) surface. Compared to active learning baselines, our method achieves higher model accuracy in fewer training iterations.

items.title: Graph Cascades: Contagion-Based Mesoscopic Rewiring for Structure-Aware Graph Machine Learning
items.description: arXiv:2606.05046v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Graph Cascades, a mesoscopic rewiring strategy for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Graph Transformers (GTs) that captures intermediate-scale graph structure beyond purely local edges or fully global attention. Using contagion-based diffusion with fixed cascade parameters, Graph Cascades constructs, in O(|V|+|E|) time, a sparse auxiliary graph where node pairs supported by repeated multi-hop reinforcement are promoted to direct neighbors. We theoretically characterize when reinforcement-based rewiring helps: sufficient conditions under which reinforcement-based edge selection is more label-aligned than direct adjacency, a stochastic block model (SBM) witness in which two-hop reinforcement is perfectly homophilic, and a formalization of mesoscopic connectivity via graph effective resistance. Empirically, across node-classification benchmarks, Graph Cascades improves multiple GNN and sparse-GT backbones, with the most reliable gains observed on heterophilic and moderate- to high-degree homophilic graphs. The theoretical conditions also identify regimes where mesoscopic rewiring is unlikely to be beneficial---low-degree regular graphs and graphs with structural bottlenecks---and these predictions match the observed failures. We additionally observe tight correlations between performance and structural properties in the rewired graphs, suggesting that rewired graphs carry predictive signals.

items.title: Theory-Scale Auto-Formalization of Logic for Computer Science
items.description: arXiv:2606.26525v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Auto-formalization is critical for scalable formal verification, but existing progress largely focuses on isolated statements, while theory-scale auto-formalization, which coherently translates hundreds of interdependent definitions, lemmas, and theorems, remains open due to challenges in consistency, faithfulness, scalability, and correctness. In this paper, we introduce LCS-Bench, a stand-alone, theory-scale benchmark based on Logic for Computer Science. LCS-Bench is built through a novel semi-automated agentic pipeline that leverages concept graphs, formal signature planning, issue tracking, sorry-filling with counter-example search, complemented by faithfulness review from human experts. The resulting artifact covers 327 textbook items, over 4,076 Lean declarations, and more than 85K lines of Lean code. The dataset supports broad evaluation through a data engine that automatically derives five tracks of evaluation benchmarks, measuring different aspects of auto-formalization and theorem-proving capabilities. We also introduce a novel evaluation protocol featuring definitional equivalence checkers, enabling more fine-grained and faithful assessment. Through extensive evaluation on 17 models, we demonstrate that (1) LCS-Bench is of high quality, consistent, and faithful; (2) the benchmark is challenging, with state-of-the-art models achieving only 20.3% on auto-formalization tasks; and (3) our analysis reveals key findings regarding theory-scale auto-formalization and suggests promising directions for future work.

items.title: Annealed Gibbs Measures with Data-Driven Interaction Potentials on Hierarchical Structures
items.description: arXiv:2606.30064v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We construct annealed Gibbs measures on continuous interaction parameters and binary spins on Cayley trees of order $k\geq 1$, with coupling functions determined by an empirical loss. The interaction parameters and spins are distinct random variables: the former determine edge couplings, while the latter represent binary labels. The training data specify the coupling function and the joint Gibbs specification, rather than automatically selecting a unique Gibbs measure on interaction parameters. We derive necessary and sufficient compatibility conditions for the finite-volume joint densities. These conditions take the form of nonlinear integral equations for boundary laws and characterize the splitting annealed Gibbs measures constructed here. For $k=1$, the translation-invariant equations reduce to positive compact integral operators. Under the stated hypotheses, they have a unique normalized positive solution. For $k=2$, an explicit empirical-loss kernel reduces the translation-invariant equations to polynomial equations. In this case, we show that hierarchical learning systems may exhibit phase-transition phenomena: for certain empirical kernels on Cayley trees order two, multiple Gibbs measures on spins emerge beyond a critical inverse temperature, corresponding to distinct equilibrium prediction regimes. For a selected annealed Gibbs measure, we distinguish its marginal on interaction parameters from its conditional Gibbs measures on spins at fixed interaction parameters. Our results provide a new perspective on energy-based learning, where data do not merely determine an optimal model through minimization but define an entire probabilistic landscape of possible inference states.

items.title: When Candidate Pools Miss Active Constraints: Evidence from Electromagnetic and Thermal Design
items.description: arXiv:2608.18903v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Finite candidate pools can limit surrogate-assisted design when good designs lie near intersecting active constraints. For independent uniform candidates in a normalized box, the typical minimum sum of gaps to k active bounds scales as (k!/N)^(1/k) for a pool of size N. This geometric limitation persists even with an accurate surrogate. We examine it through a controlled synthetic study and two finite-element design problems with inexpensive analytic constraints: a seven-variable electromagnetic coil and an independent six-variable heat spreader. The budget permits 25 initial observations and 50 further evaluations. On ten matched seeds, replacing pool EI with continuous constrained EI refinement raises mean coil response from 0.9120 to 0.9745 mT and lowers mean thermal resistance from 12.688 to 11.905 K/W. Standard continuous LogEI performs better than this refinement on nine coil seeds and all ten thermal seeds, reaching 0.9770 mT and 11.860 K/W. GP-mean search has the highest nominal coil mean but exhibits a thermal outlier on one seed. Mesh and domain checks preserve the substantial continuous-search advantage over the pool; they do not establish a resolved physical ranking among the closely performing continuous policies. Together, the sampling analysis and matched simulations identify when finite-pool search restricts the use of an FEM budget. The results support continuous constrained acquisition search, with stable LogEI as an effective existing implementation, when finite pools poorly represent high-value boundary designs. Bayesian optimization; acquisition optimization; active constraints; simulation-driven design; finite-element method; Gaussian-process surrogate; electromagnetic coil design; heat conduction

items.title: Fairness-Aware Test-Time Prompt Tuning
items.description: arXiv:2608.25707v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-language models have displayed remarkable capabilities in multi-modal understanding and are increasingly used in critical applications where economic and practical deployment constraints prohibit re-training or fine-tuning. However, these models can also exhibit systematic biases that disproportionately affect protected demographic groups and existing approaches to addressing these biases require extensive model retraining and access to demographic attributes. There is a clear need to develop test-time adaptation (TTA) approaches that improve the fairness characteristics of pretrained models under distributional shift. In this paper, we evaluate how episodic TTA affects fairness in CLIP classification under subpopulation shifts and develop FairTPT, a novel fairness-aware episodic TTA method that jointly minimizes target marginal entropy while maximizing spurious marginal entropy through soft-prompt tuning. We find that standard episodic TTA generally exacerbates disparities between majority and minority groups, that blinding a model to spurious attributes without degrading target performance is inherently challenging, and that excessive blinding can lead to catastrophic forgetting. This model collapse can be prevented by monitoring test-time changes in target loss within the linear regime, while still achieving fairness improvements on reactive data and preserving overall performance. FairTPT outperforms all state-of-the-art episodic test-time debiasing methods and establishes a foundation for robust TTA, which is essential for achieving fairness in practice.

items.title: Dandelion: A Spherical Flower for Neural Simulation of Planetary Dynamics
items.description: arXiv:2608.27521v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many dynamical processes unfold on the sphere but the default scientific machine learning architectures are Euclidean. Applying these architectures on a regular lat--lon grid causes problems: Cartesian convolutions become distorted at high latitude; 2D FFTs in Fourier neural operators incorrectly assume double periodicity; Cartesian positional encodings in ViTs distort spherical geodesic distances. Recent work moves towards natively spherical primitives, including spherical convolutions (e.g., DeepSphere or DISCO), Spherical Fourier Neural Operators (SFNOs), and geodesic attention. Here we propose Dandelion, a spherical version of Flower---a warp-based neural PDE solver. A Dandelion layer computes a tangent-plane displacement and then transports features along great circles. We obtain a U-Net-like structure by implementing hierarchical pooling entirely in the spherical-harmonic domain. There are thus no convolutions: spatial mixing is achieved only through spherical coordinate changes---or warps. To compare Dandelion with existing spherical architectures, we release an evolving benchmark suite of challenging, natively spherical PDE datasets including a modified Galewsky jet, anomalous chained turbulence, Cahn--Hilliard decomposition, spherical Riemann shocks, Held--Suarez dry atmospheric transport and global ocean dynamics. This new benchmark fills the gap between existing spherical datasets which are either too small and stylized, or much too large (ERA5) for model iteration. Dandelion achieves the best performance on all but one benchmark setting, where the best model is Flower2D, also based on warps. The spherical primitives result in the most physically consistent forecasts.

items.title: Feature Selection for Tabular Foundation Models: Exploring Feature Utility in Low-Data Molecular Prediction
items.description: arXiv:2609.30789v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Choosing features is difficult with few labeled molecules, even for a tabular foundation model that learns in context. We study this problem with TabPFN for low-data molecular property prediction, separating input width, feature meaning, and predictive usefulness while keeping contexts, query molecules, and predictor settings matched. On ADME/Tox assays from Therapeutics Data Commons, endpoint-matched assay predictions improve a compact RDKit descriptor baseline, and a provenance audit shows that most audited query molecules already occur in the predictors' training sources. Across 77 FS-Mol development tasks and 157 held-out test assays drawn from ChEMBL, broad RDKit descriptor and fingerprint families provide a strong default, rank-averaging TabPFN with support-fitted fingerprint forests improves upon both models, and learned weighting of family predictions adds further gains at a larger prediction budget. A utility-trained selector builds a traceable 16-column input from 238 sourceassay predictors, improving upon the baseline while trailing wider representations and equalwidth structural SVD coordinates. Named outputs identify what each feature predicts and where it comes from. Their usefulness for a new assay is assessed alongside the other input features, and paired removal and replacement tests measure what each selected output contributes. Together, these studies offer a protocol for evaluating feature selection, representation choice, and data provenance with a fixed tabular foundation model for few-shot molecular property prediction.

items.title: ScAn-Bench: Evaluating Scaling Analysis Methodology
items.description: arXiv:2609.35707v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent progress in machine learning is driven by large-scale foundation models, where scaling laws and finding optimal scaling prescriptions for architecture, data, and hyperparameters are key in advancing the state-of-the-art. Therefore, it is surprising that no systematic study evaluates the methodology to obtain scaling laws and prescriptions across different model types. To shed light on this crucial blind spot and facilitate future research, we introduce the surrogate benchmarks ScAn-Bench-LLM and ScAn-Bench-VLM based on 4524 and 8024 checkpoints of language and vision-language model pipelines. On our benchmarks, we perform the first systematic evaluation of both data acquisition and extrapolation methodology for scaling analysis across different data modalities.

items.title: Where Root Cause Analysis Fails: A Retrieval-Reranking Decomposition
items.description: arXiv:2609.36686v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Identifying the root cause of an anomaly among hundreds of sensors is critical for preventing safety incidents and costly downtime in complex monitored systems. Existing studies evaluate root cause analysis (RCA) methods using top@k accuracy. We show that this metric has a fundamental blind spot: it conflates two failure modes, retrieval failure, where the true cause is never considered, and reranking failure, where it is considered but ranked too low. In this work, we introduce a retrieval-reranking decomposition and audit four well-known benchmarks to expose this blind spot. Our experiments show that, on industrial CPS benchmarks, the statistical baseline scoring every sensor mis-ranks the true cause 79-100% of the time, and graph-based methods never clearly beat the best statistical baseline, whether their causal graphs are learned on short fault windows, on retrieved candidate pools guaranteed to contain the cause, or on multi-day normal-operation data. Meanwhile, on microservice benchmarks, where each injected fault drives the faulty service's own metric far above its baseline, retrieval is nearly solved (98-100%). Guided by the decomposition, we build a two-stage pipeline combining a multi-signal retriever with an LLM reranker that, as one fixed configuration, matches or exceeds the best baseline's top@1 accuracy on all six benchmark suites (by up to +12 points), with no causal graph or labeled data required. When all methods rank the same retrieved candidates with the true cause guaranteed present, adding a short system-description document lets the reranker lead the best baseline by +7 to +18 points on every benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/DecompRCA.

items.title: ElectrolyteFM: Unifying Electrolyte Property Prediction through Cross-Property Knowledge Learning
items.description: arXiv:2609.39340v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Electrolyte formulation design requires balancing multiple physicochemical properties, yet existing models often focus on a limited subset. Learning each property in isolation can overlook transferable chemical information, whereas indiscriminate sharing can introduce cross-property interference. Our directed transfer analysis shows that jointly learning two property prediction tasks can improve or degrade prediction relative to separate training, with asymmetric transfer effects between the tasks. We propose ElectrolyteFM, a unified multi-property prediction model which can more accurately predict multiple properties of each electrolyte by effectively identifying and utilizing property-specific features and knowledge shared across properties. More specifically, ElectrolyteFM learns property-specific representations independently and captures cross-property knowledge through a separately trained expert pool. A router selects relevant shared information for each formulation and target property, and property-specific residual adapters convert this information into corrections to the corresponding representation for prediction. Experiments on Electrolyte12 show that ElectrolyteFM reduces normalized mean absolute error averaged across 12 electrolyte properties by 14.8% relative to the strongest electrolyte-specific baseline. On an independent sodium-electrolyte dataset unseen during training, it reduces conductivity mean absolute error by 6.7% relative to the best-performing baseline.

items.title: One pool, many targets: a conservation layer and what archival data can identify
items.description: arXiv:2610.00445v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pairwise guide-transcript scores do not enforce conservation of a finite guide-loaded RISC pool when they are interpreted independently as occupancies. We formulate a differentiable scalar equilibrium layer: one conservation equation with a unique positive root and exact implicit gradients. It yields a redistribution theorem, a qualified high-resource limit, an analysis of the retrieval approximation, and a conditional rank-invariance result: within one construct at one dose, rankings by fractional occupancy cannot distinguish equilibrium from independent scoring. We therefore audit the two experiments that proposition leaves open, dose and cross-context, on archival off-target data. Corrected thermodynamic affinities associate weakly with measured repression in the direction a working predictor requires, but a paired permutation test and a construct-cluster bootstrap do not establish added predictive value from the coupling: what survives their differing permutation-null baselines is 0.0026, which is 2.55 paired-null standard deviations from that baseline (p=0.010) and favours independent scoring. The dose fits are heterogeneous and frequently violate the model-implied exponent constraint, which is superlinear rather than sublinear, so these data do not identify the competition parameter. A saturable compression of the competitor set holds both accuracy targets on held-out guide families but is not faster at the size measured. The contribution is a reusable conservation operator and the experimental information needed to test it. Code, result files and the data manifest: https://github.com/shadi97kh/One-Pool-Many-Targets

items.title: Trust the Direction, Search the Step: Zero-and-First-Order Methods for LLM Fine-Tuning
items.description: arXiv:2610.02190v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Step-size selection remains a central challenge in large-scale neural network optimization; conservative steps slow convergence, while aggressive steps can destabilize it. We combine Zero-and-First-Order optimization (ZFO) and propose a lightweight framework that decouples direction selection from step-size. ZFO uses a trusted first-order optimizer to determine the direction and performs zeroth-order evaluations only along this one-dimensional subspace to choose how far to move. Using the current {gradient information} and two additional objective function evaluations, ZFO instances construct a local model of the objective function along the proposed direction and select a curvature-aware step within a bounded search interval. This yields an adaptive step-selection mechanism that costs less than a full line search. We provide theoretical guarantees to show that shared-sample evaluations produce reliable finite-difference curvature estimates, that the induced local model selects a near-optimal step along the search interval, and that ZFO converges to a neighborhood of a stationary point. Across the evaluated settings, language models and datasets, ZFO frequently improves optimization and final performance relative to fixed-step first-order baselines, with the magnitude and preferred local model depending on the objective. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/nizswan/Zeroth-First-Order-Framework.

items.title: OVAL: Output-Aware Local Page Bases for KV Cache Compression
items.description: arXiv:2610.06686v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-context decoding, whether over long reasoning traces, long videos, or robot episodes, is increasingly limited by the memory of the key-value (KV) cache. Page-retrieval sparse attention makes each decoding step cheaper by attending only to the top-scoring KV pages. However, it still stores every page exactly, and adds a small digest per page for scoring, so the cache ends up slightly \emph{larger} than the full cache. We propose OVAL, which stores each page as a pair of output-aware low-rank bases that act as both the retrieval index and the storage. A key basis scores the page and rebuilds its keys when the page is selected, and a PCA basis rebuilds its values. The exact pages can then be dropped, and nothing extra is added to the cache. The key idea is that the key basis should be output-aware. A low-rank error in the keys perturbs the attention output at first order, but perturbs the page mass that retrieval ranks only at second order in expectation. OVAL therefore builds the key basis from a mix of key geometry (key PCA) and the attention-output error, with a per-head mixing weight set in closed form. At the same attended budget, OVAL is best or tied-best in eight of nine long-reasoning settings. It matches FullKV on MATH500 with 66\% of its memory, is 1.25 points above the best baseline on AIME24 with 56\%, and is on par with FullKV on LongBench~v2. On \mbox{Video-MME} and LVBench, it is within 0.32 points of exact-page retrieval at the same read, while storing 53\% of the full cache instead of 103\%. Its savings also stack with quantization and token pruning: with 4-bit bases, it is within 0.25 points of FullKV at 41\% of its memory.

items.title: Do Neural PDE Solvers Learn the Right Dynamics?
items.description: arXiv:2610.06952v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural PDE solvers can achieve low prediction errors, but do they reproduce the dynamics of the systems they model? Prediction scores alone offer an incomplete answer: they measure agreement with reference solutions but provide limited insight into how errors accumulate, nearby states diverge, or extreme events arise. We propose an evaluation framework that directly examines these behaviors in deterministic and stochastic neural solvers. By evolving ensembles of nearby initial states and comparing them with direct numerical simulation, we assess three complementary aspects of learned dynamics: error formation, ensemble geometry, and extreme events. Experiments on two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow reveal limitations that conventional scores can obscure. Smaller trajectory errors can reflect weaker error amplification despite less accurate local updates. Models can match an ensemble's overall spread and effective dimension while failing to capture the spatial directions where nearby states diverge. Similarly, matching overall event frequencies can conceal failures to predict persistent extreme events. These findings show that improved prediction accuracy does not necessarily imply greater dynamical fidelity. Our framework makes this distinction measurable, providing concrete criteria for evaluating whether advances in neural PDE solvers better capture the underlying dynamics.

items.title: Dynamical Kernel Attention: Estimating the Present from a Record of the Past
items.description: arXiv:2610.24026v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-attention encodes where a past token lies, but not how its uncertainty grows with time: evidence accumulates without bound as the context grows, and nothing indicates which tokens are safe to discard. We introduce Dynamical Kernel Attention (DKA), which derives attention from robust estimation of a latent state governed by a stochastic differential equation. Under this model, each head draws bounded evidence from any context. This lets each head abstain when relevant evidence is weak, and gives each head a memory window outside which discarding tokens changes its output by a provably bounded amount. On language modeling, DKA outperforms RoPE within the training length and ALiBi far beyond it, and matches sliding-window attention with a substantially smaller key-value cache.

items.title: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion
items.description: arXiv:2610.29362v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.

items.title: Estimating aerosol particle number size distributions from PM2.5 with physics-regularized flow matching
items.description: arXiv:2610.33557v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The mass concentration of particles smaller than 2.5um (PM2.5) is cheap to measure and widely monitored, whereas the particle number size distribution (PNSD) requires costly instruments and is measured at only a few research stations. Yet many aerosol effects, such as vapor uptake, cloud droplet formation and deposition in the human respiratory tract, depend on the PNSD rather than on mass. We explore whether generative deep learning models can infer the current PNSD from routine data: from the PM2.5 record and eight meteorological variables over a 24h window, a model generates an ensemble of plausible hourly PNSDs for the same window, reflecting that one mass can arise from many size distributions. Rather than proposing a single best model, we use two contrasting Finnish stations, the boreal forest site Hyytiala and the urban site Kumpula, as a controlled testbed. On it, we benchmark six generative models against deterministic regression and historical-mean baselines, locally and after transfer between sites, and test physical constraints for neural network training. Flow matching performs best overall; its guided variant has the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at both sites. A constraint based on a reduced aerosol general dynamic equation (GDE) lowers the CRPS by 5.5-11.5% at the training site and reduces errors after transfer between sites. Transfer remains harder than local estimation, identifying multi-station training as the next step towards PNSD estimates at unmonitored locations. This benchmark establishes physics-informed generative models as a promising route from routine air-quality monitoring to size-resolved aerosol information.

items.title: Alpha-TCM: Auditable Knowledge Integration for Multimodal TCM Inference
items.description: arXiv:2610.38754v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge-guided multimodal systems need a way to measure how supplied knowledge affects predictions, including when that knowledge is wrong. Alpha-TCM addresses this problem for traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) through an implemented workflow that separates measurements, supplied knowledge, predictions, and reviewer decisions. Observations and contextual knowledge enter separately, and a replaceable prior allows controlled interventions with fixed modality encoders. Bayesian committee accounting removes the reference prior already contained in each encoder before inserting contextual knowledge. A fully simulated confirmation study uses ten paired seeds and four training sizes. Knowledge context reduces prediction error relative to knowledge-free fusion at 600 and 1,200 training cases; equal-information learned context is competitive at 600 and has lower error at larger sizes. Controlled corruption identifies overconfident and displaced priors as the most damaging challenges. Case-level conflict detection remains weak, and training-time prior regularisation shows no consistent benefit. Functional tests verify the connected workflow separately from predictive performance. The simulation demonstrates how Alpha-TCM measures knowledge dependence, separates it from gains due to additional context, and exposes harmful prior assumptions before clinical evaluation.

items.title: Seeing Is Not Enough: Knowledge-Grounded Active Inquiry from Uncertain Visual Evidence
items.description: arXiv:2610.38774v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Similar tongue findings can accompany different syndromes in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), with decisive symptoms absent from the photograph. We present a framework for tongue assessment in which image and pulse findings guide targeted symptom inquiry and acquired answers refine the syndrome shortlist before reporting. Image/pulse predictions guide selection from a sourced symptom question bank. Known answers update the assessment used to select the next question. A calibrated loss of support for the initial prediction triggers reassessment; a subsequent report requires fresh answers supporting a stable candidate. Question and answer records make these decisions inspectable. We construct 2,600 cases from distinct real tongue photographs, assigned syndromes, simulated symptom responses and rendered pulses; 2,599 enter five-fold source-disjoint evaluation and one is training-only. On clean images, image/pulse prediction alone achieves 46.4% fine-syndrome accuracy. At acquisition cost 12, inquiry without image/pulse evidence reaches 34.4%, whereas their combination reaches 65.8% accuracy and 90.8% top-three inclusion. A same-prior, training-optimized static order reaches 59.4% and 87.3%, respectively. In a 200-case visual-training intervention within the same bank, the first question changes in 46.7% of cases and the inquiry NLL-cost curve improves. Component comparisons distinguish these acquisition gains from the coverage-cost tradeoff of reassessment. These controlled results support image-guided acquisition of missing symptoms for ranked TCM decision support.

items.title: Forecasting How RLHF Responds to Reward-Model Edits Before Training
items.description: arXiv:2611.03244v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Responses with headers, lists and greater length receive high scores from reward models (RMs), and RLHF policies learn to produce these features even when true quality does not improve. Practitioners therefore edit their RMs, but they learn whether an edit works only after an RL run. We show that the response of a policy to an RM edit can be forecast before training, from samples of the current policy and the scores of the old and new RM. If we read the RM as a set of prices, the first-order theory of KL-regularized RL implies that each feature moves in proportion to its within-prompt covariance with the change in reward. We implant controlled price changes into retrained RMs under a 2^(4-1) fractional factorial design with a self-distilled placebo, run 54 RL runs from six parent policies, and fix every forecast before the runs. With the covariance predictor, we predict the direction of all 20 changes in supply whose forecast has the same sign at every parent and explain 82% of the standardized change. With counterfactual prices, the classical alternative, we explain 50%. The forecast also holds under GRPO and for real RM upgrades, where we explain 66% out of sample with a coefficient frozen from the factorial runs. For rent, the gap between the proxy reward and a gold reward from stronger judges, we rank RM edits correctly with the same covariance over the first 30 steps (Spearman 0.94). This measures the horizon of the forecast: by step 200, the ranking of the factorial edits reverses under both RLOO and GRPO, while the real upgrades keep their order. When we vary the KL coefficient beta, the initial response does not depend on beta, and the response saturates below the KL equilibrium. In one experiment, the long-run response to a price rise is consistent with an additional implicit regularizer beta_0 of about 0.003 to 0.007.

items.title: Thought-deciphering via hierarchical EEG-to-text alignment
items.description: arXiv:2611.03623v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Non-invasive brain-to-text interfaces offer alternative communication pathways for people with communication disabilities. However, sentence-level decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) remains challenging. We propose a hierarchical EEG-text alignment framework that retrieves previously unseen sentences by progressively decoding coarse-grained semantic information and fine-grained sentence representations. We hypothesize that broader semantic context can be more reliably captured from EEG than individual sentences. Accordingly, EEG representations are first classified into semantic classes, which are defined as groups of related sentences, followed by sentence retrieval within the predicted class. Among over 2,000 unique text samples, our approach achieves, on unseen sentences, average top-5 and top-10 retrieval accuracies of 62.6\% $\pm$ 1.0\% and 83.5\% $\pm$ 1.0\%, respectively, compared with 0.3\% $\pm$ 0.3\% and 0.5\% $\pm$ 0.2\% for direct EEG-sentence alignment without semantic classification. Qualitative analysis further reveals that decoding performance depends strongly on textual context. These findings demonstrate the potential of hierarchical semantic alignment for advancing sentence-level EEG-to-text decoding.

items.title: NovoCRF: Globally Normalized De Novo Peptide Sequencing on a Prefix-Mass Lattice
items.description: arXiv:2611.05260v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: De novo peptide sequencing has moved from dynamic programming over hand-designed or generative scores to large transformers that learn the task end to end. We present NovoCRF, a conditional random field (CRF) whose states are prefix masses, so that its paths are exactly the peptides within $\pm$0.06 Da of the precursor mass. A small network scores each edge from physics-derived ion-match features and is trained with its scores globally normalized over all mass-feasible peptides. To our knowledge, NovoCRF is the first de novo method trained with exact normalization over all mass-feasible peptides. Our model has 3.6M parameters and trains in about 27 GPU-hours. Because it is small, NovoCRF can also adapt to each run at inference time: it fine-tunes part of its weights on the run's own confident answers, recalibrates the run's precursor and fragment masses, and uses retention time, predicted with a pretrained indexed-retention-time model, as further evidence. On nine held-out data-dependent acquisition datasets, NovoCRF has the highest peptide recall on five, and the transformer model InstaNovo on the other four. Where the spectrum determines the peptide, on labels with at most one peptide bond without a b or y ion, NovoCRF outperforms RNovA, $\pi$-PrimeNovo and CasanovoV5 on every dataset and InstaNovo on six of nine. The transformer models lead where many fragment ions are missing, and there their recall is up to 29 points higher on peptides of their own training data than on other peptides, while NovoCRF's recall differs least between seen and unseen peptides. NovoCRF also searches modifications it was never trained on at their exact mass: on a public spike-in of peptides with non-natural residues it finds 69.2% of the labeled spectra, against 64.4% for RNovA. With a GPU it sequences 203 spectra/s in its default two passes, and on the CPU alone it still sequences 67 spectra/s.

items.title: Regularization Amplifies Subliminal Learning
items.description: arXiv:2611.10397v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent work has shown that hidden biases can be transferred through data with no apparent semantic relationship to those biases. Can regularization limit this covert influence? By constraining adaptation, regularization might be expected to suppress behavioral changes on seemingly unrelated inputs. We systematically study this hypothesis in subliminal learning, as well as in related settings of covert influence, including phantom transfer and logit-linear selection. We find the opposite: regularization amplifies the transfer of hidden biases. In particular, subliminal learning is typically absent under full fine-tuning, but low-rank adaptation or explicit penalties can induce strong transfer. Phantom transfer and logit-linear selection show similar trends. Adding more data, an implicit form of regularization, also strengthens covert influence. Together, these findings suggest that the simplicity biases induced by regularization may facilitate covert influence. We further hypothesize that the level of regularization that maximizes covert transfer depends on task complexity.

items.title: Dual-Core Tensor Wheel Decomposition with Structure-Cached Acceleration for Tensor Recovery
items.description: arXiv:2611.13938v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tensor wheel decomposition captures complex correlations in high-dimensional data through interactions between outer-ring factors and a high-order central core. However, updating these components requires the explicit construction and manipulation of large-scale matrices, which limits computational efficiency and incurs particularly high computational and memory costs for the central-core update. To address these limitations, we propose dual-core tensor wheel decomposition (DCTW), which factorizes the central core into two lower-order cores linked by a shared latent bond. Each core is coupled to a different group of outer-ring factors. We further propose a structure-cached acceleration strategy that avoids explicit large-scale matrix multi- plications and caches intermediate tensors generated during tensor network contractions for reuse across block updates. This reuse reduces redundant computation and avoids the explicit construction of large matrices. Complexity analysis and experiments show that the strategy based on structural caching accelerates optimization compared with explicit and implicit up- date schemes while limiting the increase in peak memory as the ranks grow. Experiments on color video completion and robust denoising show that DCTW matches or outperforms representative tensor network methods in reconstruction quality, computational efficiency, and scalability.

items.title: AI4Plasma I: Data-Efficient Surrogate Modeling of Capacitively Coupled Plasma Fields
items.description: arXiv:2611.15002v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reference capacitively coupled plasma (CCP) simulations provide spatially resolved plasma fields but are costly to generate across operating conditions. We compare the data efficiency of five surrogate architectures--Coordinate MLP, PCA-Net, U-Net, Fourier neural operator (FNO), and Transolver--for predicting RF-cycle-averaged electron density, ion density, electric potential, and electron temperature in 1D planar and 2D axisymmetric GEC CCP benchmarks. We assess the number of reference simulations needed to achieve 1% and 2% mean relative L2 error for parameter-interior and parameter-boundary test cases, and examine architecture-specific mechanisms. FNO achieves the lowest or joint-lowest reference-case requirement in seven of eight comparisons. In 1D, FNO reaches 1% interior error with 50 training cases, compared with 100 for Transolver and 200 for U-Net. In 2D, FNO and U-Net each reach 1% interior error with 100 cases; FNO and Transolver each reach 2% parameter-boundary error with 200 cases, compared with 400 for U-Net. At the stricter 1% 2D parameter-boundary target, Transolver requires 400 cases versus 800 for FNO. Additional analyses investigate FNO spectral modes and padding, U-Net skip connections, Transolver adaptive slicing, and PCA-Net projection versus prediction error. The results support FNO as a data-efficient baseline for the tested CCP settings, while showing that the preferred architecture depends on the accuracy target and operating-parameter region.

items.title: AI4Plasma II: Geometry-Aware Surrogate Modeling for Variable Electrode Gap GEC Plasmas
items.description: arXiv:2611.15584v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Industrial plasma process development requires broad exploration of operating and geometric parameters. Geometric parameters, particularly electrode spacing, affect discharge structure and processing uniformity. Exploring these parameter spaces through repeated high-fidelity simulations can be computationally expensive. Surrogate models can offer rapid predictions, but geometric variation complicates their application because the computational domain and discretization may change across samples. In this work, six geometry-aware surrogate models based on prescribed and learned geometry mappings, extended-domain representation, continuous coordinates, and geometry-native discretizations are compared in terms of their data requirements for accurate predictions of full plasma fields and ion density profiles near the wafer. The simulation dataset spans pressure, voltage, frequency, and electrode gap, with each reference case requiring an average simulation cost of 5.32 CPU h. To achieve a 2% mean error across the four plasma fields, prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO and Transolver require 100 training cases, compared with 250-1000 for the other models. Predicting ion density profiles near the wafer is more demanding and reveals larger differences among models, with prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO requiring the fewest training cases for the profile accuracy targets considered. To further reduce the data required for accurate predictions near the wafer, we introduce charge-separation weighting into the training loss, which reduces the prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO's minimum tested training requirement for a 5% profile error from 1000 to 100 cases. These results support prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO as a practical starting point for the variable-gap problem studied here when a suitable geometry mapping is available, while Transolver achieves the highest prediction accuracy with sufficient training data.

items.title: SLICES: A Benchmark and Evaluation Framework for Self-Supervised Learning on Sparse ICU Time Series
items.description: arXiv:2611.18868v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) results for intensive care unit (ICU) time series are hard to compare when data processing, encoders, and adaptation vary together. We present SLICES, a benchmark and evaluation framework for comparing and extending SSL methods under a shared clinical setup. It fixes 24-hour value and observation-mask inputs, a Transformer encoder, patient-level splits, four endpoints, two adaptation protocols, and five matched seeds across MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD, and their pooled union. Masked autoencoding (MAE), joint-embedding prediction (JEPA), and contrastive learning provide reference implementations. Among these objectives, MAE leads mean AUPRC in all nine frozen classification comparisons, also under converged probes, and in seven of nine fine-tuning comparisons. Fine-tuned MAE leads hospital mortality at full labels and scores higher than a supervised Transformer of the same architecture at every label fraction, and SSL fine-tuning gives the lowest length-of-stay error. Supervised baselines remain strong elsewhere: GRU-D leads 24-hour mortality and XGBoost leads acute kidney injury in all three regimes. Rankings depend on the adaptation protocol, the comparator set, and whether the probe loss matches the metric. A two-seed MIMIC-IV rerun with the maintained code stays within two across-seed SDs of the reference in all 48 downstream runs. The code repository supports new objectives, shared downstream evaluation, and regeneration of the reference results, so new SSL methods can be compared with these references under the same conditions. Generalization to unseen hospitals is not tested here and is the natural next extension.

items.title: VASR: Vector-Aware Assembly Planning with Equivalent Structures and Repair-Cost Feedback
items.description: arXiv:2611.20984v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Furniture assembly planning requires inferring subassembly hierarchies from individual parts and a target illustration. Existing raster-based methods do not explicitly exploit the geometric and structural information in SVG drawings. We introduce VASR, a framework that fuses features from a dedicated SVG encoder with visual representations from a pretrained vision-language model to predict assembly hierarchies. To avoid penalizing valid alternatives to a reference assembly tree, we propose Repair-Aware Hierarchical Policy Optimization (RHPO) with hierarchy-preserving equivalence rewards. RHPO further uses repair-cost feedback to favor decisions with lower downstream correction costs among candidates with comparable equivalence-aware rewards. VASR achieves the highest Equivalent-Hard F1 among the evaluated methods, outperforming GPT6-Astra by 17.69 percentage points on the IKEA-derived test set while maintaining strong performance on an independent furniture dataset.

items.title: Multiply Robust Causal Mediation Analysis with Continuous Treatments
items.description: arXiv:2105.09254v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In many applications, researchers are interested in the direct and indirect causal effects of a treatment or exposure on an outcome of interest. Mediation analysis offers a rigorous framework for identifying and estimating these causal effects. For binary treatments, efficient estimators for the direct and indirect effects are presented by Tchetgen Tchetgen and Shpitser (2012) based on the influence function of the parameter of interest. These estimators possess desirable properties such as multiple-robustness and asymptotic normality while allowing for slower than root-n rates of convergence for the nuisance parameters. However, in settings involving continuous treatments, these influence function-based estimators are not readily applicable without making strong parametric assumptions. In this work, utilizing a kernel smoothing approach, we propose an estimator suitable for settings with continuous treatments inspired by the influence function-based estimation strategy. Our proposed approach employs cross-fitting, relaxing the smoothness requirements on the nuisance functions and allowing them to be estimated at slower rates than the target parameter. Additionally, similar to influence function-based estimators, our proposed estimator is multiply robust and asymptotically normal, allowing for inference in settings where parametric assumptions may not be justified.

items.title: Nanorobot queue: Cooperative treatment of cancer based on team member communication and image processing
items.description: arXiv:2111.11236v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Although nanorobots have been used as clinical prescriptions for work such as gastroscopy, and even photoacoustic tomography technology has been proposed to control nanorobots to deliver drugs at designated delivery points in real time, and there are cases of eliminating "superbacteria" in blood through nanorobots, most technologies are immature, either with low efficiency or low accuracy, Either it can not be mass produced, so the most effective way to treat cancer diseases at this stage is through chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Patients are suffering and can not be cured. Therefore, this paper proposes an ideal model of a treatment method that can completely cure cancer, a cooperative treatment method based on nano robot queue through team member communication and computer vision image classification (target detection).

items.title: High-Dimensional Tail Index Regression
items.description: arXiv:2403.01318v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Motivated by the empirical observation of power-law distributions in the credits (e.g., ``likes'') of viral posts on social media, we introduce a high-dimensional tail index regression model and propose methods for estimation and inference of its parameters. First, we propose a regularized estimator, establish its consistency, and derive its convergence rate. Second, we construct a debiased version of the regularized estimator to facilitate inference and prove its asymptotic normality. Monte Carlo simulation studies corroborate our theoretical findings. We apply these methods (1) to the text analysis of viral posts on X (formerly Twitter) and (2) to the analysis of abnormally high health expenditures.

items.title: Scalable Learning from Probability Measures with Mean Measure Quantization
items.description: arXiv:2502.04907v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider statistical learning problems in which data are observed as a set of probability measures. Optimal transport (OT) is a popular tool to compare and manipulate such objects, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when the measures have large support. We study a quantization-based approach in which all input measures are approximated by $K$-point discrete measures sharing a common support. We establish consistency of the resulting quantized measures. We further derive convergence guarantees for several OT-based downstream tasks computed from the quantized measures. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves performance comparable to individual quantization while substantially reducing runtime.

items.title: Quantum Cognition Machine Learning for Forecasting Chromosomal Instability
items.description: arXiv:2506.03199v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The accurate prediction of chromosomal instability from the morphology of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) enables real-time detection of CTCs with high metastatic potential in the context of liquid biopsy diagnostics. However, it presents a significant challenge due to the high dimensionality and complexity of single-cell digital pathology data. Here, we introduce the application of Quantum Cognition Machine Learning (QCML), a quantum-inspired computational framework, to estimate morphology-predicted chromosomal instability in CTCs from patients with metastatic breast cancer. QCML leverages quantum mechanical principles to represent data as state vectors in a Hilbert space, enabling context-aware feature modeling, dimensionality reduction, and enhanced generalization without requiring curated feature selection. QCML outperforms conventional machine learning methods when tested on out of sample verification CTCs, achieving higher accuracy in identifying predicted large-scale state transitions (pLST) status from CTC-derived morphology features. These preliminary findings support the application of QCML as a novel machine learning tool with superior performance in high-dimensional, low-sample-size biomedical contexts. QCML enables the simulation of cognition-like learning for the identification of biologically meaningful prediction of chromosomal instability from CTC morphology, offering a novel tool for CTC classification in liquid biopsy.

items.title: First-order methods for stochastic and finite-sum convex optimization with deterministic constraints
items.description: arXiv:2506.20630v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we study a class of stochastic and finite-sum convex optimization problems with deterministic constraints. Existing methods typically aim to find an $\epsilon$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, in which both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are within a prescribed tolerance $\epsilon$. However, in many practical applications, constraints must be nearly satisfied with certainty, rendering such solutions potentially unsuitable due to the risk of substantial violations. To address this issue, we propose stochastic first-order methods for finding an $\epsilon$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($\epsilon$-SFSO) solution, where the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $\epsilon$ and the expected optimality gap is at most $\epsilon$. Our methods apply an accelerated stochastic gradient (ASG) scheme or a modified variance-reduced ASG scheme $only\ once$ to a sequence of quadratic penalty subproblems with appropriately chosen penalty parameters. We establish first-order oracle complexity bounds for the proposed methods in computing an $\epsilon$-SFSO solution. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed methods.

items.title: Mix-Opt: Mixed Optimization for Memory-Efficient Personalization of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
items.description: arXiv:2507.10029v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Memory-efficient personalization is essential for adapting text-to-image diffusion models while preserving user privacy and operating within the limited computational resources of edge devices. To this end, we propose Mix-Opt, a novel mixed optimization framework that adaptively chooses between backpropagation on low-resolution images (BP-low) and zeroth-order optimization on high-resolution images (ZO-high), guided by the characteristics of the diffusion process. As observed in our experiments, BP-low efficiently adapts the model to target-specific features but suffers from structural distortions due to resolution mismatch. Conversely, ZO-high refines high-resolution details with minimal memory overhead but faces slow convergence when applied without prior adaptation. By complementing both methods, our framework leverages BP-low for effective personalization while using ZO-high to maintain structural consistency, achieving memory-efficient and high-quality fine-tuning. To maximize the efficacy of both BP-low and ZO-high, we introduce a timestep-aware probabilistic function that dynamically selects the appropriate optimization strategy during training. This function mitigates overfitting from BP-low at high timesteps, where structural information is critical, while ensuring that ZO-high is applied more effectively as training progresses. Experimental results across both U-Net- and DiT-based diffusion models demonstrate that Mix-Opt achieves competitive personalization performance while significantly reducing memory consumption. Mix-Opt enables scalable, high-quality personalization without modifying the inference process or increasing inference latency.

items.title: An open dataset of gas adsorption in deformable metal-organic frameworks for direct air capture
items.description: arXiv:2508.03162v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Engineering economical and scalable processes for direct air capture (DAC) from humid air relies on atomistic modeling to search and identify promising sorbent materials from a vast chemical space. Machine learning has emerged as a powerful tool for predicting material properties in an efficient yet accurate manner, but these models require large sets of carefully curated training data. We present the Open DAC 2025 (ODAC25) dataset comprising nearly 60 million DFT single-point calculations for CO2, H2O, N2, and O2 adsorption in ~15,000 MOFs. ODAC25 introduces functionalized MOFs, high-energy adsorbate placements, and synthetically generated frameworks to maximize the versatility of models trained on the dataset. ODAC25 improves upon the accuracy of DFT calculations in previous works and applies engineering intuition from recent work regarding the treatment of adsorbate-induced MOF flexibility. We release state-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on ODAC25 and demonstrate their utility via Henry's coefficient predictions. ODAC25 enables MOF screening for DAC at a resolution previously unattainable.

items.title: JigSLO: Solving the Resource Puzzle for Efficient Multi-LLM Serving
items.description: arXiv:2509.06261v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: GPU spatial sharing co-locates instances with complementary demands, such as compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode, promising cost-efficient multi-LLM serving. Prior systems partition compute and coordinate shared memory capacity, but do not model bandwidth contention among co-located instances of heterogeneous LLMs. This contention makes each instance's latency depend on the memory-access patterns of its co-runners, even when its own resource allocation remains unchanged. Drawing on extensive measurements, we find that the latency impact of bandwidth contention can be captured by a time-shared memory-access model with contended and uncontended periods, so the overall latency can be analytically estimated as a time-weighted average of the latency estimates for these periods. We propose JigSLO, a contention-aware multi-LLM serving system that manages memory resources and schedules each model's prefill and decode phases as separate instances, treating their co-location as a placement decision. Its contention-aware predictor estimates per-instance latency under any co-location from standalone profiles alone. Guided by these predictions, its placement algorithm jointly selects each instance's tensor parallelism, compute share, and batch configuration, pairing complementary memory-access patterns to maximize throughput within each model's latency targets. JigSLO's shared resource manager complements this on the capacity side, sharing weights, pooling KV cache, and transferring it between prefill and decode instances. Across three datasets covering chat, code generation, and long-context summarization, JigSLO outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by $2.3\times$ in SLO attainment and $1.2\times$ in throughput on average, matching their best attainment with half the GPUs on long-context workloads.

items.title: SURFing to the Fundamental Limit of Jet Tagging
items.description: arXiv:2511.15779v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Beyond the practical goal of improving search and measurement sensitivity through better jet tagging algorithms, there is a deeper question: what are their upper performance limits? Generative surrogate models with learned likelihood functions offer a new approach to this problem, provided the surrogate correctly captures the underlying data distribution. In this work, we introduce the SUrrogate ReFerence (SURF) method, a new approach to validating generative models. This framework enables exact Neyman-Pearson tests by training the target model on samples from another tractable surrogate, which is itself trained on real data. We argue that the EPiC-FM generative model is a valid surrogate reference for JetClass jets and apply SURF to show that modern jet taggers may already be operating close to the true statistical limit. By contrast, we find that autoregressive GPT models unphysically exaggerate top vs. QCD separation power encoded in the surrogate reference, implying that they are giving a misleading picture of the fundamental limit.

items.title: A physics-constrained neural solver for incompressible flows without labeled data
items.description: arXiv:2511.18820v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a physics-constrained neural solver for incompressible flow that requires neither labeled data nor supervised pretraining. The solver enforces incompressibility and boundary conditions (BCs) to strict tolerances. We attribute the limited Reynolds numbers of existing physics-informed approaches to insufficient enforcement of these constraints, on which conventional finite-difference and finite-volume solvers depend. We therefore formulate incompressible flow as a constrained optimization problem within the physics- and equality-constrained artificial neural network (PECANN) framework: the pressure Poisson residual is minimized subject to the momentum equations, continuity equation, and BCs imposed as equality constraints on the primitive variables, while a conditionally adaptive augmented Lagrangian method enforces each constraint. The pressure Poisson objective proves critical. Across all benchmarks, replacing it with the momentum residual fails to converge to accurate solutions under identical architecture and constraint enforcement, which we attribute to the global elliptic coupling of pressure and velocity that local momentum-residual minimization lacks. For advection-dominated flows, we introduce an adaptive vanishing entropy viscosity that stabilizes training while leaving the converged solution unchanged. The solver predicts lid-driven cavity flow up to Re = 7,500 with centerline velocity profiles matching benchmark data, and is further validated on flow over a backward-facing step at Re = 800, 3D unsteady Beltrami flow, and steady and unsteady flow past a circular cylinder under an inflow-outflow configuration, for which an ablation study identifies admissible outlet BCs for velocity and pressure. From a randomly initialized network and without external perturbations, the solver captures the spontaneous onset of periodic vortex shedding in unsteady cylinder flow.

items.title: On the use of case estimate and transactional payment data in neural networks for individual loss reserving
items.description: arXiv:2601.05274v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The use of neural networks trained on individual claims data has become increasingly popular in the actuarial reserving literature. We consider how to best input historical payment data in neural network models. Additionally, case estimates are also available in the format of a time series, and we extend our analysis to assessing their predictive power. In this paper, we compare a feed-forward neural network trained on summarised transactions to a recurrent neural network equipped to analyse a claim's entire payment history and/or case estimate development history. We draw conclusions from training and comparing the performance of the models on multiple, comparable highly complex datasets simulated from SPLICE (Avanzi, Taylor and Wang, 2023). In environments where covariate data is limited, we find evidence that case estimates will improve predictions substantially, but that equipping the neural network with memory only leads to meagre improvements. Although the case estimation process and quality will vary significantly between insurers, we provide a standardised methodology for assessing their value.

items.title: A Cherry-Picking Approach to Large Load Shaping for More Effective Carbon Reduction
items.description: arXiv:2601.17990v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Shaping multi-megawatt flexible loads such as data centers alters generator dispatch on the electric grid, affecting system-wide CO2 emissions and wholesale electricity costs. However, evaluating prevalent load-shaping signals - such as grid-average carbon intensity, locational marginal price, renewable generation, or commercial marginal emission estimates - has remained difficult because full-scale market-clearing models and generator bid data are rarely accessible outside system operators. Here we conduct year-long causal dispatch counterfactuals using a calibrated, nearly 8,900-bus replica of ERCOT's day-ahead Security Constrained Unit Commitment and Security Constrained Economic Dispatch market-clearing process across renewable-rich and fossil-dominated zones. We find that while LMP-based shaping outperforms other static signals in annual grid CO2 reductions, no single signal performs best across all operating conditions. Motivated by these insights, we propose an interpretable daily "cherry-picking" strategy that selects among practicable day-ahead signals using observable grid net demand and nodal minimum LMP, with thresholds learnable directly from historical market data. Cherry-picking achieves 2-3 times greater annual grid CO2 savings than static LMP shaping without increasing wholesale electricity cost relative to flat operation. Extending this framework to coordinated spatial and temporal shifting across two grid nodes increases CO2 reductions by over 70% compared to temporal-only shifting. Finally, because shaping load against region-wide average carbon intensity can backfire and raise physical grid emissions in fossil-heavy zones, our findings highlight the need for Scope 2 carbon-accounting frameworks to incorporate locational, price-aware, and congestion-aware signals.

items.title: HyperKKL: Enabling Non-Autonomous State Estimation through Dynamic Weight Conditioning
items.description: arXiv:2602.22630v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper proposes HyperKKL, a novel learning approach for designing Kazantzis-Kravaris/Luenberger (KKL) observers for non-autonomous nonlinear systems. While KKL observers offer a rigorous theoretical framework by immersing nonlinear dynamics into a stable linear latent space, its practical realization relies on solving Partial Differential Equations (PDE) that are analytically intractable. Current existing learning-based approximations of the KKL observer are mostly designed for autonomous systems, failing to generalize to driven dynamics without expensive retraining or online gradient updates. HyperKKL addresses this by employing a hypernetwork architecture that encodes the exogenous input signal to instantaneously generate the parameters of the KKL observer, effectively learning a family of immersion maps parameterized by the external drive. We rigorously evaluate this approach against a curriculum learning strategy that attempts to generalize from autonomous regimes via training heuristics alone. The novel approach is illustrated on four numerical simulations in benchmark examples including the Duffing, Van der Pol, Lorenz, and R\"ossler systems.

items.title: PRUE: A Practical Recipe for Field Boundary Segmentation at Scale
items.description: arXiv:2603.27101v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large-scale maps of field boundaries are essential for agricultural monitoring tasks. Existing deep learning approaches for satellite-based field mapping are sensitive to illumination, spatial scale, and changes in geographic location. We conduct the first systematic evaluation of segmentation and geospatial foundation models (GFMs) for global field boundary delineation using the Fields of The World (FTW) benchmark. We evaluate 18 models under unified experimental settings, showing that a U-Net semantic segmentation model outperforms instance-based and GFM alternatives on a suite of performance and deployment metrics. We propose a new segmentation approach that combines a U-Net backbone, composite loss functions, and targeted data augmentations to enhance performance and robustness under real-world conditions. Our model achieves a 76% IoU and 47% object-F1 on FTW, an increase of 6% and 9% over the previous baseline. Our approach provides a practical framework for reliable, scalable, and reproducible field boundary delineation across model design, training, and inference. We release all models and model-derived field boundary datasets for five countries.

items.title: On Minimal Observation Time for Recovering Latent Hawkes Networks
items.description: arXiv:2605.08400v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dynamics of interacting systems in engineering, society, and nature often evolve over latent networks that govern which entities can interact. We study the problem of inferring these networks from event-based observations, which arise naturally in finance, seismology, and neuroscience. While there is substantial algorithmic work addressing this important problem, theoretical results are scarce. In this paper we ask the following fundamental question: what is the minimum time that one must observe the dynamics in order to exactly recover the underlying network, as a function of the number $d$ of interacting entities? For a class of stationary Hawkes processes with sparse, weak interactions, we prove that an observation time of order $\log d$ is sufficient and necessary. For the upper bound we construct a two-stage estimator that uses clipped and binned event data for screening, followed by a least-squares refinement, and apply concentration bounds derived from the Poisson cluster representation. For the lower bound we combine Fano's inequality with Jacod's Girsanov formula for point processes on a suitable subclass of networks.

items.title: Measuring and Decomposing Mode Separation via the Canonical Diffusion
items.description: arXiv:2605.08777v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mode separation, namely how sharply a distribution fragments into barrier-separated clusters, is a fundamental geometric property of densities, difficult to quantify in high dimensions. Modes are often the meaningful alternatives in the data, such as the conformations of a molecule or the distinct semantic types among a generative model's outputs. Mode separation is distinct from dispersion, which is what standard label-free tools capture: differential entropy rises with spread regardless of fragmentation, and PCA orders directions by variance regardless of barriers. Mutual information does capture it, but only given the latent component labels, which are usually unavailable. We measure mode separation through a single stochastic process intrinsic to the density, namely the unique reversible diffusion with $f$ as its stationary distribution and a constant scalar diffusion coefficient. From its autocovariance matrix we extract two readouts. The first, SSA (Sum of Squared Autocorrelations), is a scalar barrier-sensitive measure. The second, DA (Dominant Autocorrelation directions), gives linear projections ordered by metastability rather than variance. Under an isotropic-Gaussian null, we derive the limiting spectrum of the empirical autocovariance in closed form, generalizing the Marchenko--Pastur law. Its upper edge gives a noise floor that separates metastable directions from sampling noise. Both readouts use only samples and a score function, scaling to high dimensions through pretrained score-based generative models via Tweedie's identity.
