items.title: How ArisGlobal scaled generative AI inference on Amazon Bedrock
items.description: ArisGlobal, a provider of life sciences technology spanning pharmacovigilance, regulatory, medical affairs, clinical, and quality functions, developed NavaX, an AI engine purpose-built for life sciences on Amazon Bedrock , to automate adverse-event case processing. ArisGlobal chose Amazon Bedrock for managed access to foundation models, EU geographic cross-Region inference, and managed prompt caching. As enterprise customers added distinct compliance requirements, the shared prompt prefix grew by about 150% over 6 months, while per-case inference costs increased by more than 200%. ArisGlobal first cached each source document because it was the largest part of a request. That left the growing shared prompt prefix outside the cache. By reversing the order and caching the shared prefix instead, ArisGlobal reduced effective input cost and supported additional tenants without proportional cost growth. Who is ArisGlobal? ArisGlobal is the creator of LifeSphere, a unified SaaS platform for pharmacovigilance, regulatory affairs, quality, and medical information. LifeSphere serves pharmaceutical companies globally, including multiple Top 20 pharma organizations by revenue (source: ArisGlobal press release ). The entire system runs on AWS. LifeSphere NavaX is ArisGlobal’s AI engine that transforms drug safety from a system of record into a system of strategic advantage. ArisGlobal productionized their first generative AI solution on Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic’s Claude in March 2025. According to ArisGlobal’s internal production telemetry, they have processed over 1 million real transactions in regulated pharmaceutical environments, handling billions of tokens across multiple enterprise tenants. Model availability varies by Region. See Model support by AWS Region . How NavaX processes an adverse event case When a pharmaceutical company receives an adverse-event report, typically a multipage PDF describing a patient’s reaction to a medication, NavaX’s Dynamic Data Extraction (DDE) agent extracts around 130 fields. These fields include patient demographics, suspect drugs, reporter information, event timelines, seriousness criteria, and regulatory classifications. Because this content includes protected health information, ArisGlobal applies responsible-AI controls as a standard part of its production deployment. It draws on capabilities such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter content and detect or mask sensitive information. Extracted fields are also validated against the schema and grounded in the source document. This extraction happens across multiple sequential requests to the model. Each request focuses on a different section of the case form, and each carries: System instructions — model behavior rules, output format specifications, and regulatory compliance constraints. Customer-specific rules — per-tenant extraction logic, field mappings, and business rules that differ by pharmaceutical company. Extraction schema — around 130 target fields with types, validation rules, and few-shot examples. The source document — the adverse event PDF (often 10–200 pages). Two inputs repeat at different scopes. The shared prompt prefix includes the system rules, extraction schema, and few-shot examples. It repeats across requests, cases, and tenants using the same agent. The source document repeats only for the requests associated with one case. The prompt bloat problem When NavaX launched with its first enterprise tenant, the system prompt was lean. As ArisGlobal onboarded additional pharmaceutical companies, each brought specific requirements: Custom field mappings (Tenant A maps reaction onset differently from Tenant B). Regulatory jurisdiction rules (EU ICSR compared with FDA MedWatch and PMDA formatting). Company-specific business logic for seriousness assessment and causality. Per-tenant few-shot examples calibrated to each company’s historical cases. Over 6 months, the shared prompt prefix grew from approximately 72,000 to 180,000 tokens, a 150% increase. With multiple sequential requests per case, per-case inference costs increased by more than 200%. The prefix grew with every tenant and was reprocessed on every request, so prompt growth compounded with transaction volume. Table 1 compares the original document-first request order with the production prompt-first design. Aspect First approach Production design Request order Per-case document, cache checkpoint, shared prompt prefix Shared prompt prefix, cache checkpoint, per-case document Cached prefix The document, which changes for every case The shared prompt prefix, which repeats across requests Reuse scope Only the remaining requests for one case Requests across cases and tenants using the same agent Cost effect The growing prompt is repeatedly processed at the full input rate Fleet-wide prompt reuse supports sublinear cost growth EU routing EU geographic cross-Region inference remains unchanged EU geographic cross-Region inference remains unchanged Amazon Bedrock prompt caching strategies Amazon Bedrock prompt caching reduces latency and input token costs by caching a contiguous prompt prefix from the start of a request through a cache checkpoint. A later request with the same prefix can read cached tokens at a reduced rate instead of processing them again. Cache entries have a time-to-live (TTL) that resets after a successful cache hit. Caching is prefix-based rather than block-based. Request sections are evaluated in sequence—tools, system, then messages—so changing an earlier section invalidates matching content that follows it. Cache checkpoints (explicit control) With explicit cache checkpoints, you can choose the exact prefix boundary. Supported Claude models allow up to four checkpoints per request. items.description: Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life. To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled "Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech" on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki , a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts. Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans. items.title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
items.description: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge. It’s “worse than a bug” Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.” Read full article Comments

items.title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
items.description: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue? Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication. Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N . N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors. VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N 2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N 2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N 2 . In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N , not N 2 . So the energy used will scale as N , not N 2 , as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied. Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10 -19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10 -14 and 10 -12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000. But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements. McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.” It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law .

items.title: llm 0.37.3
items.description: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code . Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp : That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp

items.title: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab
items.description: At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. A Supercomputing Lab on Any Desk The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 20TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems. The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures. Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control. What Researchers Can Do With It The kit opens up new possibilities for researchers. Researchers can explore agent-assisted workflows that prepare simulation inputs, launch runs and summarize results, while the scientists validate the setup and conclusions. Researchers can also train AI models that approximate slow simulations, then use them to refine wing designs toward minimum drag. Before committing supercomputer time, a team can narrow a 10-million-cell simulation to the 50-500 dimensions that matter. Kvantify is using NVIDIA cuQuantum, and reports running tensor-network simulations of quantum-chemistry circuits with up to 70 qubits and 975 gates on a single DGX Spark, benchmarking circuits generated for penicillin ground-state energy calculations. CYRAN AI , an IIT Delhi spin-out, uses DGX Spark and its PixelFlux library to accelerate JPEG 2000 decoding for large satellite images, supporting local geospatial analysis. OpenFold shows how researchers can fine-tune OpenFold3 on NVIDIA DGX Spark to improve protein-ligand structure predictions for drug discovery. The Rubin Lab at IGI at University of California, Berkeley is using a DGX Spark and NVIDIA Evo 2 model to predict bacterial traits directly from genome sequences by comparing embeddings from genomic and protein language models against the classical baselines. With no 11-hour cluster queue times, results arrived 15x sooner on DGX Spark. The Hartwig Group at UC Berkeley is using a DGX Spark to perform LoRA fine-tuning on the Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B model for chemistry machine learning, training a prediction head on experimental values. By running locally on the Spark using NVFP4 quantization, the lab successfully fit a 120B-class model on a single device and bypassed multi-day cluster queue times, allowing them to run continuous eight- to 24-hour training fits back-to-back. Where to Find the Kit The developer kit is on display at SC26 and available for sale. DGX Spark products and cables can be purchased from top OEM partners and are also available through NVIDIA Marketplace . Partners include Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, H3C, HP, Lenovo, MSI and xFusion. An NVIDIA playbook for building and running the NVIDIA HPC SDK, a software development kit for scientific computing, is coming soon. Once available, it will give scientists and researchers a local platform to develop multi-node GPU applications, explore FP32 and mixed-precision algorithms and run molecular dynamics and materials simulations using LAMMPS with Kokkos before scaling to data center systems. Learn more about NVIDIA DGX Spark . Subscribe to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter . Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X , Instagram , TikTok and Facebook . See notice regarding software product information. items.title: Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse
items.description: A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza. Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC . The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak , supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago. This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons. items.title: Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
items.description: Users of a knowledge-grounded application expect it to remember them, not only to search well. They ask follow-up questions that make sense only in the context of the previous turn. They expect an answer about a policy or a procedure to reflect what they told the application about themselves last month. And they still expect every answer to be grounded in the documents they are allowed to read, with citations. Whether the application is a customer support assistant, a document chat inside a SaaS product, or an internal assistant over company policies, the expectation is the same. Meeting that expectation is hard, because the context that would sharpen a search lives outside the knowledge base. A user’s location, role, or product tier was often mentioned in an unrelated conversation weeks ago. To use it, the application has to store every conversation, extract durable facts from it, decide which facts matter for the current question, and inject them into the request. When many users share the application, every one of those steps also has to be isolated per user, and so does every document. Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , now take over these steps: storing each conversation, extracting facts from it, and bringing the relevant facts into the search. You turn this on by adding a memoryConfiguration to the AgenticRetrieveStream request, which makes AgentCore memory a retrieval source alongside your knowledge base. Within the same call, the service restores the conversation, and the planner decides on its own when a fact about the user would help. It retrieves that fact from long-term memory and uses it to compose the sub-queries it sends to the knowledge base. After generating the answer, the service saves the turn back to memory. The same request carries a userContext , so the knowledge base returns only the documents that the user’s access control lists (ACLs) allow. The integration is opt-in and backward compatible. Your application keeps only what is genuinely yours: authenticating the user and passing who they are. This post shows how to build such an assistant for many users who share one knowledge base and one memory resource. Each user sees only the documents they may read, and each user’s memory stays private. The running example is an internal employee assistant for AnyCompany, a fictional company. Employees sign in with Amazon Cognito and ask questions over HR policies, IT guides, engineering runbooks, and sales plans. We show how to read the user’s identity from the Cognito ID token, how to pass it to AgenticRetrieveStream for document ACLs and for memory, how to design memory namespaces for many users, and how to read the trace to see when the planner used memory. Finally, we make AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) enforce per-user memory isolation even when application code gets it wrong. If you deployed the application from Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base , this post replaces its “persist conversation history yourself” step. Solution overview AnyCompany keeps its documents in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). One managed knowledge base syncs them through an ACL-enabled Amazon S3 data source. A global ACL file in the same bucket says which employees may read each folder: everyone reads HR and IT, only engineers read the engineering runbooks, and only salespeople read the commission plan. One AgentCore memory resource is shared by every employee. Amazon Cognito authenticates employees, and its ID token supplies two claims: the sub (user ID) identifies the user’s memory, and the verified email identifies the user to the knowledge base’s ACL filter. Three test users sign in: two engineers, Maya and Liam, and one salesperson, Sofia. The trace excerpts in this post are taken from a run of the sample application in the GitHub repository . Figure 1: Architecture of the memory-aware employee assistant. The application authenticates the user and constructs the request (steps 1–4). Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base restores the session, retrieves information, returns an answer, and saves the exchange to AgentCore memory (steps 5–8). Short-term events and long-term records belong to the same memory resource. The employee signs in with Cognito and receives an ID token, a JSON Web Token (JWT) signed by the user pool. The application’s API validates the token — an Amazon API Gateway JWT authorizer in production, a small FastAPI service in the sample. Unauthenticated requests do not reach the handler. The handler reads two claims from the verified token: sub becomes the memory actorId and namespace, and email becomes the userContext.userId . The client body carries only { question, sessionId? } . The handler then assumes the application’s IAM role for this user, with the session tag userId= . The handler calls AgenticRetrieveStream with the knowledge base as the retriever, userContext , and a memoryConfiguration bound to this user. Managed Knowledge Base restores the conversation history from short-term memory (STM) in AgentCore memory for the actor and session identified by sessionBinding . Managed Knowledge Base retrieves from the knowledge base with ACL filtering based on userContext . It can also retrieve the user’s configured long-term memory through speculative retrieval or memory searches selected by the planner. Managed Knowledge Base streams a cited answer and trace events back to the handler. The handler records the traces with a correlation ID and forwards the answer and trace information to the UI. With persistenceMode: DEFAULT , the service saves the question and generated answer to the session. AgentCore memory then extracts long-term records asynchronously according to the configured strategies. Figure 2: One AgenticRetrieveStream turn with userContext and memoryConfiguration . items.title: How Duco transforms financial data automation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: Financial institutions face a critical challenge: processing massive volumes of data with speed, accuracy, and compliance while operating under some of the world’s strictest regulatory frameworks. Duco is the agentic Operations platform for financial services, serving tier-one banks and other financial institutions. It processes 20 billion transactions monthly for 200+ clients, including 7 of the top 20 banks and 10 of the top 20 asset managers. To keep pace as data processing demands grew, Duco evolved from traditional machine learning models to the agentic AI capabilities of Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. In this post, we share how Duco rebuilt its agentic AI stack on these services, cutting deployment time and onboarding costs while keeping each bank’s data isolated. The challenge: Scaling intelligence in a regulated environment Duco’s platform empowers teams to automate mission-critical data processes using AI and no-code models, handling everything from data extraction to downstream publication. It already used traditional machine learning models for predictive labeling and pattern recognition, helping banks consolidate and automate over 20,000 processes. However, these classical machine learning approaches had inherent limitations. They required extensive historical data for training, struggled with novel scenarios, and demanded significant customization for each new use case. Most critically, they couldn’t adapt quickly to the diverse, constantly evolving data formats and business rules that characterize modern financial operations. “The classical prediction models worked to an extent, but they weren’t agile or flexible enough. Traditional machine learning models can only amplify what they’ve already learned — they can’t help with the next step or find new problems.” — Rob Gates, Chief Architect and Innovation Officer, Duco The solution: Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore Duco made a strategic decision to adopt Amazon Bedrock for managed access to foundation models, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to run agents at scale. This was more than a technology upgrade. It was a fundamental shift in how its system could understand, reason about, and act on financial data. About Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers a choice of high-performing foundation models from leading AI companies through a single API, along with a broad set of capabilities to build generative AI applications with security, privacy, and responsible AI. Learn more about Amazon Bedrock . Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale. Build with any open source framework and any model. Connect agents to your tools and data with authentication and access controls built in. Monitor and improve agents in production with tracing and evaluation. AgentCore handles the infrastructure so you focus on agent logic, not backend plumbing, and you get enterprise security and reliability without giving up open source flexibility. Learn more on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore product page. Why Amazon Bedrock? Several factors made Amazon Bedrock the ideal choice for Duco’s regulated financial services industry (FSI) environment: Security and compliance first: With Amazon Bedrock, customer data stays within the AWS environment, and it is not used to train models. With private endpoints in its virtual private cloud (VPC), Duco can connect to internal systems while keeping them completely isolated, which matters for sensitive financial data processing. Model flexibility: Access to leading foundation models from the Amazon Nova 2 family, Anthropic, OpenAI, Cohere, Meta, and Mistral AI through a single API means Duco can choose the right model for each task. Duco can switch between models by changing a configuration parameter. Built for financial services: Amazon Bedrock provides the robust governance controls and compliance frameworks that financial services require, avoiding infrastructure complexity while maintaining the security standards tier-one banks demand. Choosing AgentCore as the runtime Duco’s existing agent infrastructure was built on LangChain and LangGraph, both of which were already in production. When evaluating runtime options for its agentic workloads, AgentCore emerged as the clear choice for three key reasons: Compatibility with existing primitives: AgentCore is fully compatible with Duco’s existing LangChain and LangGraph code, so most existing code continued to work without modification. Managed runtime: Instead of Duco running its own agent infrastructure, AgentCore provides a fully managed runtime, reducing operational overhead for the engineering team. Regulated environment suitability: AgentCore met the stringent requirements of deploying in regulated financial services environments, with built-in security and compliance controls. Multi-tenant architecture: Isolation by design Duco’s platform operates as a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) offering with strict tenant isolation (figure 1). This is a non-negotiable requirement for regulated institutions. The architecture reflects this at every layer, from the underlying cloud infrastructure right up to the AI agent runtime. Figure 1: Multi-tenant architecture Infrastructure layer Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) clusters with namespace-per-tenant isolation and network segregation help maintain workload separation at the Kubernetes layer. Per-tenant dedicated AWS services : every tenant receives a dedicated Amazon Aurora MySQL database, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) storage bucket, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption keys, Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) messaging stack, Amazon ElastiCache layer, and Amazon Cognito user pool. Zero shared data infrastructure across clients. Per-tenant autoscaling helps minimize the impact of one client’s compute-intensive workload

items.title: Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing
items.description: Enterprise teams are building multi-agent systems, and when early implementations fall short, the cause is rarely the model. Multi-agent coordination is a distributed systems problem, and many teams taking it on haven’t yet built distributed systems instincts. The numbers are consistent across sources: ~88% of AI pilots never reach production . Stanford HAI demonstrated that two models can perform worse collaborating than either alone when coordination overhead exceeds the benefit. The pattern is clear: teams are adding complexity faster than they build understanding. Ten steps that are each 95 percent reliable deliver only 59.9 percent end-to-end reliability, and 20 steps deliver 35.8 percent. This illustrative model assumes a strictly sequential chain with no retries, but the direction holds: each dependent handoff multiplies risk. In this post, you learn how to decide whether a use case needs multiple agents, choose a coordination pattern, and spot costly anti-patterns early. You also see how takt time, safety boundaries, edge data, and shift cycles shape the architecture. Multi-agent coordination patterns Coordination patterns fall into two tiers, based on who controls the flow. In Tier 1, you define the path. In Tier 2, the model chooses the path at runtime. That flexibility handles work whose steps you can’t define in advance, at a higher cost in tokens, latency, and debugging. The practical default is to start with Tier 1 and move a task to Tier 2 only when its subtasks emerge during the work. Tier 1: Patterns (deterministic control flow) 1.1 Sequential Pipeline: Orchestration patterns that implement linear execution where each node’s output feeds into the next node (A -> B -> C) supporting ordered processing with predictable execution timing In the following diagram, input flows to agent A (extract), then agent B (transform), then agent C (validate), and then output. The user defines that order at build time, and nothing is decided at runtime. As a result, the pipeline is straightforward to debug and test, and its cost is predictable. Typical fits include document processing, extract, transform, and load (ETL) chains, and warranty-claim triage. Figure 1: Sequential pipeline where each agent’s output feeds the next, from extract to transform to validate 1.2 Conditional Workflow: Logic-based edges select the next node by condition, so the workflow can branch and send each case down a different path. In the following diagram, a user request goes to agent A (write code) and then to agent B (test code). A pass/fail check sends passing work to agent D (deploy). Failing work loops back to agent A for a retry, up to a maximum of N times, and then escalates to a human. The orchestration layer enforces that cap, for example through an AWS Step Functions iteration limit, which keeps the loop from becoming the unbounded iteration anti-pattern described later in this post. Figure 2: Conditional workflow that retries failures up to N times before escalating to a human 1.3 Conditional Router : A classification step examines the input and directs it to the appropriate processing path. Only one path is executed per request. Best for intent-driven dispatch, quality-gate decisions, customer inquiry routing, and anomaly triage. The following diagram shows a plant supervisor’s request being read by a classifier and sent to exactly one specialist. Questions about whether parts meet spec go to the Quality Agent, overdue equipment services go to the Maintenance Agent, and shift changes go to the Scheduling Agent. This decision is made at the entry point. Figure 3: Conditional router that runs one path per request, with bounded retries before human escalation 1.4 Parallel Workflow: A task splits into independent subtasks that run simultaneously across handlers, each on its own data. A fan-in step combines the results when all handlers complete, and a failure in one path retries only that path. Best for multi-source analysis, batch processing, and work that decomposes into independent pieces. In the following diagram, a research orchestrator decomposes the task and dispatches it to three specialist agents that run concurrently: a financial data agent, a geopolitical agent, and a logistics agent, each analyzing its own source. A combined step waits for all three, then synthesizes the results, resolves conflicts, and ranks the findings. Latency equals the slowest single agent rather than the sum of all three. Figure 4: Parallel fan-out to specialist agents followed by a fan-in step that synthesizes and ranks the results Tier 2: Autonomous patterns (LLM-determined control flow) In autonomous patterns, control flow is determined at runtime by the AI model itself, not predefined by developers. Agents read task state, reason about what’s needed and coordinate through shared context rather than fixed paths spanning a spectrum from structured orchestration to fully emergent behavior. 2.1 Plan-based orchestration In plan-based orchestration, a single orchestrator agent acts as a project manager. The orchestrator maintains an explicit task plan with assignments and dependencies, sees all context while each worker receives only its slice, distributes work dynamically against the current plan, and monitors progress centrally. Key design choice is that the workers are stateless and independent. If one fails, it doesn’t contaminate others. The orchestrator retries only the failed worker, not the entire workflow. The following diagram shows how a planner agent decomposes a task into an explicit plan and dispatches each step to a worker’s agent. Each step goes to a dedicated worker (a research agent, an analysis agent, and a report agent) that sees only its assigned slice. Figure 5: Plan-based orchestration with a planner agent assigning each step to a stateless worker agent 2.2 Handoff pattern Agents operate with limited, local knowledge and coordinate through peer-to-peer delegation. items.title: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips
items.description: On the heels of the Nvidia scandal , the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training. In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop "more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.” Read full article Comments

items.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
items.description: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress. On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell. But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good. The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

items.title: How MoEngage built agentic customer engagement on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: This post was co-written with Ashwin Srinivasan, Nishan Das and Karthik Baile from MoEngage. A marketing or product team member planning a weekend flash sale often opens three tools before writing a single line of copy. First they open the analytics dashboard to see what worked last time, then the content library to find the right tone, and then the campaign builder to build the campaign itself. Repeat that across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp, and much of a marketing team’s week goes to navigating tools instead of making decisions. The MoEngage Model Context Protocol (MCP) Connector gives an MCP-compatible assistant, such as Claude or ChatGPT, secure, tenant-scoped access to a brand’s segments, campaign history, and content library. This capability points to a broader shift in software platforms. Beyond a user interface for business users and an API for engineering teams, a third layer is emerging, where a user describes an outcome in plain language and an agent carries out the steps across the platform. For a customer engagement platform, that means a capability already exposed as an API can become a tool an agent calls, and a campaign that once moved across several tools can move through one conversation instead. MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use across channels including push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and Rich Communication Services (RCS), set out to build this layer. MoEngage built Merlin AI, a set of artificial intelligence (AI) agents that work with live platform data. Marketing and product teams can now draft, analyze, and adjust campaigns from a single conversation, while agents decide what to send each customer. One customer, Glance, saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates as a result. MoEngage treated this as an architecture problem. The question was how to give agents secure, tenant-scoped access to live data without rebuilding hundreds of existing APIs. In this post, we walk through how MoEngage solved it with Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale with any framework or model. The post covers the four agent modes in Merlin AI, how MoEngage exposed its existing APIs as MCP tools, and how the architecture keeps each tenant’s data isolated. It closes with the results MoEngage customers have seen and the pattern other software providers can reuse. Solution overview: Four agent modes in Merlin AI Merlin AI runs four kinds of agents. All four share the same foundation: foundation models in Amazon Bedrock for reasoning and generation, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for hosting, and MCP for standardized access to data. Across all four modes, Merlin AI uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, tool-call planning, and content generation. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock . Embedded agents in Merlin AI Studio Merlin AI Studio places purpose-built agents at the exact point in the workflow where marketing and product teams do that piece of work: Copywriter generates personalized push and transactional copy that stays consistent with the brand voice. Designer produces a marketing banner or image from a text description. Segment Assist turns a plain-language audience description into the correct set of attributes and filters. For example, a marketing or product team member can ask for users who abandoned a cart in the last 2 hours. Jinja Assist converts natural-language requests into working Jinja and Liquid markup for dynamic content. In-app Template Builder creates responsive, accessible HTML templates for in-app messages, including gamified formats, lead-capture pop-ups, and surveys. Flow Assist turns a high-level idea into a ready-to-deploy customer journey. Behind the scenes, a sequence of specialized steps interprets the request, proposes paths, builds the flow structure, refines it with historical data, and packages it for deployment. Conversational agents Conversational agents work across campaigns, analytics, segments, and flows. A user can ask a question in plain language and the agent calls the right tools to answer it or act on it. The Campaign Insights Agent, embedded on the analytics page, delegates to specialized sub-agents. One sub-agent runs analysis across several metrics at once. A second diagnoses why a metric is underperforming, and a third compares performance across time periods or segments. A final step formats the findings into a clear answer. Custom agents Custom agents let lifecycle and customer relationship management (CRM) teams design agents that run continuously on MoEngage data and tools, inside rules the product and marketing team defines. Every agent shows its work through an activity log of the data it pulled, the decisions it made, the channels it touched, and the content it sent. Teams can run an agent with full autonomy or require human review before anything executes. Decisioning agents Decisioning agents act for each individual customer. Each agent decides what to say, when, how often, and on which channel, and it learns from every outcome. Product and marketing teams set the content, goals, and guardrails, and the agents handle the rest, with visibility into every decision. Offer Decisioning selects the best offer on web and app surfaces. Campaign Decisioning delivers 1:1 decisions across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp. Together with workflow agents, this puts both halves of agentic marketing in one system. Architecture overview The architecture has four layers. Each layer has a single responsibility and can change without affecting the others. Clients. items.title: Modernizing mainframe Assembler to Java using Amazon Bedrock and AWS Transform
items.description: Imagine a batch job that has run every night for decades without failing, and the only person who understands its code is about to retire. We have seen this situation again and again while working with banking, insurance, and airline customers. Their Assembler programs still run critical business operations, but fewer people can read them each year. Rewriting them by hand takes years, risks breaking business rules nobody remembers writing, and still depends on the same experts who are leaving. Amazon Bedrock and AWS Transform change that equation. This post shows you a multi-stage transformation methodology using Amazon Bedrock , Kiro IDE (an AI-powered integrated development environment), and AWS Transform that can help reduce modernization time compared to manual approaches while maintaining business logic integrity through validation checkpoints. You will learn how to systematically extract business rules from Assembler code, convert them through an intermediate COBOL stage, and deploy modernized applications as Java Spring Boot services on AWS. Prerequisites Before starting the modernization process, make sure you have: Active AWS account with least-privilege AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for Amazon Bedrock, AWS Transform, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). Access to Amazon Q Developer or Kiro for AI-assisted code analysis. Access to AWS Transform for COBOL to Java conversion. Access to Amazon Bedrock with appropriate foundation models (FMs). An Amazon S3 bucket configured for source code and artifact storage, with encryption and Block Public Access enabled. Knowledge of the target business domain and application functionality. Availability of business and technical subject matter experts (SMEs) for validation sessions. Source Assembler code inventory with available documentation. Test data sets with expected outputs for functional equivalence testing. Solution overview You can transform legacy mainframe Assembler applications tightly bounded with COBOL into Java Spring Boot applications built for the AWS cloud through a systematic five-phase approach. This multi-stage methodology, converting Assembler to COBOL as an intermediate step before Java transformation, reduces risk and preserves business logic with greater reliability than direct Assembler-to-Java conversion. The intermediate COBOL stage provides a structured, human-readable format that subject matter experts (SMEs) can validate before final transformation. This makes sure that business rules remain intact throughout the modernization journey. The following sections describe both the current mainframe architecture and the target cloud-focused state. Current state Your current architecture represents a traditional mainframe environment where Assembler programs execute batch processes, connected with COBOL, interact with databases, and process files. At its core, JCL (Job Control Language) jobs trigger Assembler program execution at scheduled intervals. These programs read input from VSAM (Virtual Storage Access Method) and sequential files and perform operations against IBM Db2 for z/OS. Your business logic executes using low-level register operations (direct CPU register manipulation) and memory management. Output is written back to files or database tables, and job completion status is reported through JCL return codes. All of this runs on IBM z/OS mainframe infrastructure. Figure 1: Mainframe Assembler architecture Target state The modernization solution helps you transform legacy mainframe Assembler applications into Java applications built for the AWS cloud through a multi-phase, AI-powered workflow. The architecture uses Amazon Bedrock and Kiro IDE for AI-assisted code analysis and business rule extraction, and AWS Transform for automated COBOL-to-Java conversion. If COBOL source code is already available, you follow the conventional approach and provide it directly to AWS Transform for conversion to Java Spring Boot applications. With this solution, you can achieve: Reduced transformation time compared to manual approaches. Systematic business logic preservation through validation checkpoints. Human-in-the-loop validation at critical stages. Automated code conversion with functional equivalence testing. Figure 2: End-to-end Assembler-to-Java transformation architecture on AWS, showing five main phases: business rules extraction, spec-driven data flow, Assembler-to-COBOL conversion, validation, and COBOL-to-Java transformation You begin the transformation workflow by analyzing Assembler code to generate Business Rules Extraction (BRE) documentation. You then create detailed functional specifications with human-in-the-loop refinement. The validated specifications guide the Assembler-to-COBOL conversion, generating intermediate COBOL code that bridges the gap between low-level hardware instructions and business-oriented constructs. This COBOL code undergoes functional equivalence testing before AWS Transform converts it to Java, with validation checkpoints at each phase to reduce risk and verify business continuity. Business rules extraction with AI The quality of your Business Rules Extraction (BRE) directly impacts transformation accuracy, so focus carefully on this phase. Use Amazon Bedrock, through Kiro IDE or the Amazon Bedrock console, along with AWS Transform for mainframe to extract and document business rules from your Assembler source code. You can use the prompts in this post directly in Amazon Bedrock through the Chat Playground , or within Kiro IDE using its built-in AI chat and Spec panel . Replace the placeholder values with your actual Assembler code and context before running. Amazon Bedrock is the inference platform behind the first four phases: business rules extraction, specification creation, Assembler-to-COBOL conversion, and validation. items.title: Novo Nordisk modernizes manufacturing process documents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: Novo Nordisk (Novo) is one of the world’s leading global pharmaceutical companies, manufacturing medicines for chronic diseases such as diabetes and obesity, and delivering them to patients across many countries. Behind every product lies a manufacturing network that adheres to strict quality requirements. Every quality-relevant process step must be described, controlled, and validated through formal documentation. Keeping this documentation current and accurate is a core responsibility of the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area, a responsibility that spans a large and diverse portfolio of controlled documents, including standard operating procedures, work instructions, forms, and training materials, across the global organization. Managing this portfolio presents significant challenges. Document updates are frequent, driven by regulatory changes, process improvements, equipment modifications, and audit findings. Each update demands careful review, structured approval workflows, and timely communication to all affected stakeholders. With thousands of active documents spread across multiple divisions, departments, and product programs, tracking which documents are due for revision, pending approval, or require immediate attention becomes increasingly complex. Much of this oversight currently relies on manual processes and fragmented tracking methods such as spreadsheets or disconnected systems. These methods are time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to scale. The result is a risk of outdated documentation remaining in circulation, delayed updates, and critical gaps in compliance visibility. Beyond document management, there is a deeper knowledge challenge. Valuable manufacturing knowledge is distributed across many controlled documents, versions, sites, and product programs. Finding the right answer at the right time often depends on experienced individuals knowing where to look. This dependency on tribal knowledge creates bottlenecks that slow down decision-making and, ultimately, impact how quickly life-saving medicines reach patients. To address these challenges, the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area has embarked on developing an intelligent support system powered by agentic AI, deployed on AWS. The goal is to reduce lead times, improve documentation visibility, and make critical manufacturing knowledge more accessible, ultimately helping the organization move faster and serve more patients around the world. This post dives deep into the architecture and the key design decisions made to meet the high standards of accuracy and traceability required in a regulated pharmaceutical environment. The solution helped subject-matter experts (SMEs) complete work that used to take hours or days in minutes. We also describe an AI process-intelligence assistant that can answer complex process questions with grounded, cited responses. The solution is built around a GraphRAG architecture, combining a knowledge graph with hybrid search to retrieve the most relevant and contextually accurate information. AI agents, built on a managed agent framework, coordinate the retrieval and response process end-to-end. A guided mode helps clarify ambiguous questions before a search is initiated, helping make responses more precise and defensible. The challenge Teams supporting manufacturing repeatedly answer variations of the same question: what does the process require, for this site, this product, and this equipment? Answering well requires four things at once: The right document out of a large corpus. The right version and lifecycle state (approved and effective, not draft or obsolete). The right scope (it actually applies to the site, product generation, and equipment). The relationships (which documents reference which, and what a change would impact). Conventional keyword search returns documents, not answers, with no concept of scope, version, or relationship. A plain vector-based Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system improves recall on natural-language questions but still struggles with exact identifiers (document numbers, equipment codes), with multi-hop relationship questions, and (most importantly for a regulated domain) with identifying when relevant content is not available. The team needed a system that treats structure and relationships as first-class, stays grounded in approved sources, and clarifies instead of guessing. Solution overview The assistant is built on a GraphRAG architecture: a knowledge graph in Amazon Neptune captures structure and relationships, and a hybrid search index in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless provides semantic and exact-match recall over document contents. The two stores are deliberately kept separate and bridged at query time rather than combined into a single engine. This is a common production GraphRAG pattern. The reasoning layer runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore was chosen for its managed agent runtime with built-in session isolation, native tool orchestration, and integrated AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and observability. This removes undifferentiated infrastructure work so the team could focus on the domain logic. The agent runtimes are built with the Strands Agents SDK and powered by Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock . Documents are processed through an ingestion pipeline that uses Amazon Bedrock Data Automation for multimodal parsing, orchestrated with AWS Step Functions and AWS Lambda . The stack is defined as infrastructure as code with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) . At a high level, a question flows through the system like this: The query agent receives the question and, in guided mode, determines whether the scope is clear enough to answer well. items.title: AI Companies Develop Decision Models to Avoid Hallucinations
items.description: On 15 September, a startup called TypeSafe AI released a new AI model called Jev . The company’s broad, disruptive claims about Jev that turned heads: The company claimed that Jev, which it calls a “System One model” is cheaper, faster, and can’t hallucinate. TypeSafe AI’s marketing is an obvious shot across the bow of other AI companies and their large language models (LLMs), which, despite their capabilities in math and coding, are infamous for their cost and tendency to “hallucinate” factually incorrect replies. And the startup has certainly attracted both attention and investment. The company recently raised $870 million in funding at a valuation of $7.5 billion . But the most impressive metric of Jev’s success is arguably the many imitators it’s already spawned. Cloudflare, Amazon, OpenAI, and Microsoft quickly released “decision models” that imitate Jev’s capabilities. Start-ups, academic researchers, and independent enthusiasts have released dozens more. “I have to give Jev credit,” says Matt Mastracci , an independent developer who has trained and released several decision models including Djev , which Cloudflare cited as an inspiration for its own decision models . “It really brought decision models to the forefront. In six or seven weeks, we’ve seen dozens of models come out.” Jev’s Latency and Compute Advantages Most AI researchers would call Jev a decision model or decider model. TypeSafe AI’s branding of Jev as a System One model refers to a theory of cognition popularized by psychologist Daniel Kahneman in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow . In the book, Kahneman draws a line between fast, instinctive thought (System One) and slower, deliberate thought (System Two). TypeSafe AI argues that modern LLMs offer the second, but are too slow to provide the first. The company claims that Jev can provide end-to-end response latency between 70 and 500 milliseconds. By comparison, LLMs typically require at least several seconds, to provide a response, and more complicated tasks (like coding software from scratch) can take several hours. Independent testing backs up TypeSafe AI’s claims. A pre-print co-authored by Ramayya Krishnan , a professor of information systems at Carnegie Mellon University, along with several colleagues, found that Jev delivered a median latency of 150 milliseconds across several benchmarks designed to gauge decision accuracy, including RewardBench and JudgeBench . OpenAI’s most capable model at the time, GPT-6 Astra, delivered a median latency of 1.89 seconds. A faster reply is often a cheaper reply, because it requires less compute time, and that’s reflected in TypeSafe AI’s pricing. The startup charges US $0.042 per million input tokens and output tokens are free. By contrast, for GPT-6 Astra, ChatGPT charges $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Even GPT-6 Luna, a variant of GPT-6 designed for fast, inexpensive inference, costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens . Mastracci says that lower latency and costs open opportunities to tackle tasks LLMs currently can’t handle.“You can think of content moderation, such as moderating a fire hose of social media posts, or an extremely busy chat room.” Michelle Chen , a group product manager at Cloudflare (which has released its own decision models, including Clef and Claric ), is also bullish on what decision models can accomplish. “You can probably offload 80 percent of your typical LLM tasks to a System One model that is going to be so much faster and so much cheaper.” TypeSafe AI has offered few details about how Jev achieves its speed, but Jev’s open-weights imitators provide more transparency. For example, take Cloudflare’s Clef, an open-weights decision model which is free to download on Hugging Face . “With an LLM, when you’re generating an output token, it looks at all the previous tokens, and predicts the next output token,” explains Chen. This occurs in sequence, token after token, until an end token is reached. “Our decision models don’t do that. They just do a single forward pass, to generate one read of all the inputs, and then generate one output. That’s why it’s a lot faster.” How Decision Models Generalize Tasks Decision models based on an LLM, such as Clef (which is based on Alibaba’s Qwen LLM ), still contain the neurons and transformer-based model architecture of an LLM. They still input and output tokens. However, the portions of the model that turn these tokens into text have been changed to constrain the output. “Jev can only answer questions with a predefined, structured answer format,” says Zhongyu Wei , a professor at Fudan University who is also a co-author of a study that benchmarks decision models and introduces an open-weight alternative, SII-Decision . “We give it a question and options such as A, B and C, and it must choose from those options, returning probabilities alongside its choice.” In one sense, decision models are a return to classifiers , a type of model that, as the name implies, learn to sort data into classes. They’re used in a wide range of tasks, including spam filters and face detection. “These kinds of models are not new,” says Chen. “It’s almost like a rebranding.” But decision models offer a key upgrade over prior classifiers: generalization. Mastracci explains that classifiers were traditionally created through domain-specific training. Decision models, though, retain the general intelligence of an LLM, and that makes them applicable to many situations. “You can pick it up off the shelf, you point it at your problem, and it works,” says Mastracci. Cloudflare is putting this advantage into practice. Before decision models, teams looking to use a classifier model had to “get a lot of data, stand up a machine learning team, and fine-tune” a model for the task, Chen says. Decision models eliminate this requirement, so one decision model can be used in many domains. Examples include flagging spam pull requests in Cl

items.title: Get answers from tables with tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
items.description: Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports tabular search, so you can get answers from tables through agentic retrieval. When a question needs data from CSV, XLSX, or XLS files, tabular search looks up values and runs calculations across every relevant row in one or more tables or sheets. It then combines the results with facts from related documents to answer analytical questions that take several steps. A finance team closing the quarter needs to know “Which departments must write variance commentary?” No single file has the answer. It depends on the variance policy’s threshold, the quarter-close memo’s budget revisions, and math over every department in the profit and loss (P&L) workbook. Like this finance team, most teams keep their narratives and data in the same place. For example, a Microsoft SharePoint site holds workbooks next to policies, and an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket holds CSV exports next to PDFs. Tabular search answers questions across these files through the same AgenticRetrieveStream request you already use for documents. It runs code over the original file in an isolated sandbox, so the answer uses the whole table instead of only the rows that retrieval returns. For the finance team, one request returns the departments that must write commentary. The answer cites the policy and the memo, and the trace names the workbook the code read. In this post, you learn how tabular search answers questions that need both table data and facts from documents, and when another tool is a better fit. You also build a knowledge base with sample finance files and use the trace to see which file the code read. Why tables are hard for retrieval Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) returns a fixed number of passages that best match a question, which works well for prose. Tables lose information when they’re split into passages, in ways that depend on the table’s shape: Long tables – A table with thousands of rows spans many passages, and retrieval returns only the few that best match the question. An answer built from them uses a handful of rows, so a total, a comparison, or a threshold check can be incomplete. Wide tables – In a table with hundreds of columns, one row can hold more text than a passage or a search model takes in at once. As a result, values in later columns are harder to match. Long passages from wide tables can also match many unrelated questions and push more relevant passages out of the results. Retrieval also has to match a question to the right table. Questions use business terms, such as “controllable spend,” but tables hold cost center codes, account names, and numbers. A draft and a final workbook look almost the same to search. The rule that gives the numbers meaning is often in a separate document, such as a policy. Tabular search therefore splits the work. Retrieval only has to return one passage from the right table file, and code then reads the whole table. Because retrieval still has to find that file first, naming the file in your question helps. Table 1 shows how plain retrieval and tabular search each handle the finance team’s question, “Which departments must write variance commentary?” Compared Retrieve only Agentic retrieval with tabular search What you get back Passages from the policy, memo, business review, and workbook, but no complete answer An answer naming Sales, Engineering, and Operations, with each department’s variance against its revised budget Revised variance percentages Not available. No file stores them, so no passage can contain them Calculated from every department row in the final workbook Sources Each passage links to its own file, but none of them contains the answer Citations to the finance policy and the close memo. The trace names the workbook the code read Table 1: The same question with plain retrieval and with tabular search. How tabular search works in agentic retrieval In agentic retrieval , an agent uses retrieval to decide which documents matter and then writes the answer. Tabular search is part of that flow, so there’s nothing to turn on. When a question needs the data in a table, the request moves through these stages: Retrieve – Passages come back, including passages from a table file. Plan – The agent uses the question and table structure to determine whether to run code over one or more retrieved tables. Stage – Tabular search copies the original file into an isolated sandbox with no network access. Compute – Model-written code runs over the whole table or sheet. Return – The agent gets back only what the code prints, such as totals or matching rows. Answer – The agent answers from the results and the passages, with citations. Tabular search starts when retrieved passages come from a CSV, XLSX, or XLS file and the question needs a calculation across rows or a lookup of specific values. Knowledge bases, connectors, and APIs An AgenticRetrieveStream request can search one knowledge base or several. The Retrieve API keeps returning passages and doesn’t run code. Tabular search works the same way whichever connector brings the files into the knowledge base, including Amazon S3, Microsoft SharePoint, Atlassian Confluence, and others. Scope and trade-offs Tabular search is built for questions that need calculations or lookups over the table files it retrieves. Running code adds at least one more agent turn, so answers that use table data take longer than text-only answers. Governed metrics, recurring dashboards, warehouse-scale joins, and reporting controls still belong in your business intelligence (BI) tools. Tabular search works on table files stored next to your documents, and you don’t define a schema. Solution overview In this solution, an Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base stores your CSV and Excel files together with related documents, such as PDF and Word files. Your application sends every question through agentic retrieval. When a question needs table data, the answer combines cal
