Based on validation PSNR and stability across random seeds, we select the configuration that uses all three filter families, redraws filters every optimization step, and employs Gaussian initialization. We evaluate RaFL on three 2D and two 3D image reconstruction tasks. RaFL outperforms a pixel loss on three tasks and matches it on two, and demonstrates stable performance across random seeds on all five tasks. RaFL adds less than 2% to the backbone's forward FLOPs and no inference cost, requiring $182\times$ fewer loss FLOPs than a VGG19 perceptual loss. These findings suggest that RaFL is a simple, tuning-free, and domain-agnostic loss objective for 2D and 3D image reconstruction.

items.title: The Polyak-{\L}ojasiewicz Paper: A 10-Year Retrospective
items.description: arXiv:2611.17745v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In 2016, we wrote a paper introducing the phrase "Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition" for an old idea, unsure of how readers would react. The paper ultimately had a larger impact than we expected, and we are surprised and honoured to receive the 2026 PKDD ECML Test of Time Award. With 10 years of hindsight, this note offers an informal and candid retrospective on the PL condition. We take a look back at the origins of the paper, give an AI-assisted refined version of the main theorem, review criticisms of the work, and discuss a variety of related ideas and extensions.

items.title: Efficient Genotype Classification from 3D MRI in ADPKD via Density-Aware Point Sampling and E(3)-invariance
items.description: arXiv:2611.17758v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Early detection of genetic kidney diseases, especially autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), is crucial because certain genotypes such as truncating PKD1 mutations cause rapid kidney growth and early progression to end-stage kidney disease. MRI-based genotype inference is a potential low-cost complement to genetic testing. However, although many deep learning methods have been developed for classifying various MR images, applying them to ADPKD remains challenging: (1) abdominal MR images are generally too large to be handled by deep learning models designed for smaller images like brain MRI, and (2) the amount of labeled data for ADPKD genetic mutations is insufficient to train deep learning models. In order to address these challenges, we propose E3PN, an efficient 3D MRI-based ADPKD genotype classification network that relies on point sampling and E(3)-invariance. We utilize a point representation of 3D MRI, which consumes less GPU memory than a voxel representation. For further memory efficiency, 3D points are sampled from a mixture distribution over the two kidneys in each image. Since E(3)-invariance has been shown to improve data efficiency, we also incorporate it into our model through coordinate canonicalization. On our ADPKD dataset, E3PN trains 163 times faster and uses 103x less GPU memory than a 3D ResNet, while also improving F1 from 0.165 to 0.226 over both baselines. These results establish a first benchmark for five-way ADPKD genotype classification from 3D MRI and show that point sampling and coordinate canonicalization yield two-orders-of-magnitude efficiency gains with a modest but consistent improvement in F1.

items.title: Learning Anisotropic Prediction Targets for Flow Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.17767v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Flow-based generative models are trained on a hand-chosen prediction target, such as the velocity, the noise, or the clean data. This choice strongly affects training and sample quality. We introduce Anisotropic Flow Models (AnisoFlow), which replaces a fixed prediction target with a fully learnable one. AnisoFlow learns to scale the noise component of the target anisotropically, assigning a separate nonnegative weight to each direction in a jointly learned basis. A closed-form map recovers the velocity from the network's prediction, leaving the architecture, flow-matching loss, and sampler unchanged. Since recovery is exact, training optimizes the target purely to make it easier for the network to predict. We theoretically analyze the resulting prediction error and predict that the preferred noise weight in each direction scales near-linearly with data variance, in agreement with the weights learned empirically in pixel space. AnisoFlow improves FID from 1.90 to 1.55 over the JiT baseline on ImageNet 256$\times$256, by learning only the prediction target, without representation alignment or architectural changes. In pixel-space text-to-image generation, AnisoFlow improves image quality and, through better-conditioned velocity recovery, largely removes patch-seam artifacts under reduced-precision inference.

items.title: Beyond Prediction Gain: LASR as a Metric for Action-Grounded Latents in World Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.17775v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations. Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts. Existing evaluation practices---reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance---cannot isolate this distinction. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.

items.title: Hierarchical Bayesian physics-augmented neural networks for populations of hyperelastic laws: specimen variability and uncertainty from scarce, noisy data
items.description: arXiv:2611.17892v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The hyperelastic law of a material such as soft tissue differs between specimens, and often only a few specimens can be tested. Physics-augmented neural networks (PANNs) learn such laws from data without a prescribed functional form while keeping them physically admissible, and Bayesian versions of related models quantify the uncertainty of the law of one specimen or of a pooled group of specimens. A pooled fit, however, attributes the differences between specimens to measurement noise or to uncertainty about a mean law, and neither describes a new specimen. We first develop a Bayesian PANN for one specimen, whose priors keep the learned law plausible for few, noisy data. We then extend it to a hierarchical Bayesian PANN, a nonlinear mixed-effects model in which all specimens share learned polyconvex features and each specimen is a draw from a population of laws. Features, specimens, and population are inferred jointly by variational inference, with a separate model of the measurement noise, so that the variability between specimens is not mistaken for noise, the population carries its own uncertainty, and every specimen drawn from it is polyconvex. The population predicts the response of new specimens with credible intervals, without data or from a partial test, and assigns them to cohorts with quantified uncertainty, all without a prescribed form of the law. On synthetic populations, it recovers the population from few specimens and predicts new specimens more reliably than three published methods. On Treloar's rubber and on healthy and aneurysmal aortas, it reaches the accuracy of a deterministic PANN and assigns no aorta specimen to the wrong cohort with confidence, although it underestimates the uncertainty of untested curves.

items.title: Domain Adaptation Based Pipeline for Character Classification and Handwritten Text Recognition
items.description: arXiv:2611.17952v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Character classification and handwritten text recognition, particularly in specialized tasks, often suffer from limited labeled data, while a large amount of unlabeled data remains unused. To address this challenge, we propose a novel unsupervised domain adaptation-based pipeline to reduce the distribution gap between source and target domains. Our pipeline follows three main steps. In the first step, we pretrained an expert model on source data, to learn a strong general representation. In the second step, we perform unsupervised domain adaptation to leverage unlabeled target data, adapting the model to the specific characteristics of the target domain. In the third step, we trained the expert model on source data in the target style. By aligning the feature distributions between the source and target, our method enables the model to generalize effectively across diverse datasets. The unsupervised training increases the computation time only during training not in inference. We evaluate the pipeline on both character-level and historical handwritten line recognition tasks, demonstrating its flexibility. We establish a new state-of-the-art on the Safran-MNIST-DLS dataset defined in Track 2 of the DAGECC competition with 76.17% Macro F1-score and achieve competitive results on each of the specific datasets of READ 2018 without using the labels of the target data. Code is available at https://github.com/simon-corbi/DRANet-for-classification-and-htr

items.title: Efficient and Practical Clustering of Variables in Causal Graphs
items.description: arXiv:2611.17971v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clustering variables in a graph may improve visual clarity and simplify causal inference. Harnessing the full potential of clustering requires an automated method to detect useful clusters in a graph. We introduce a novel class of clusters called conduits, and present a sound, complete and efficient algorithm for detecting all conduits in the graph. In addition to algorithmic detectability, conduits appear naturally in causal graphs stemming from real-world applications, enabling substantial size reduction. Furthermore, the structure of conduits enables the application of known identifiability results regarding clustering. We demonstrate these properties in a simulation study with real-world graphs.

items.title: Algorithmic Opacity as a Principal-Agent Problem
items.description: arXiv:2611.17980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Concerns about gaming and trade secrecy, frequently invoked to justify algorithmic opacity, can also mask self-serving strategic behavior by decision-makers, who may prioritize private benefits over social welfare. We develop a principal-agent test for when algorithmic decision-making should trigger disclosure obligations even when concerns about gaming or trade secrecy exist. The test, which is anchored in decision quality, relies on two diagnostics that can be disclosed without enabling gaming or revealing trade secrets: the error profile (false positive and false negative rates, overall and for each group) and the distribution of decision outcomes across groups. These diagnostics make visible whether decision-makers align design and implementation with the public interest or instead use opacity to obscure bias, inefficiency, or strategic shirking. Strong disparities across social groups, and asymmetries in the distribution of decision errors across outcome types, should trigger rebuttable presumptions favoring further disclosure. Where ground-truth error rates are unavailable, outcome distributions across groups can support the same presumption, and a decision-maker's inability to produce an error profile is itself diagnostic. The test thus treats fairness metrics as triggers for further disclosure and extends to generative and agentic systems through analogous metrics. The framework informs differentiated disclosure regimes (staged, partial, mediated, or audience-segmented). Once such regimes are considered, the domain of justifiable algorithmic opacity is significantly narrower than commonly assumed: when gaming or trade secrecy risks are legitimate, actionable disclosures (such as training data characteristics and key system design parameters) ordinarily can be mandated without compromising innovation or enabling gaming, even for technically inscrutable algorithms.

items.title: JaRS: Contrast-Free Localization of Memorized Regions in Diffusion Models via Jacobian Row Sums
items.description: arXiv:2611.18024v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion models sometimes memorize and reproduce regions of their training images, raising privacy and copyright concerns. We aim to localize these regions. Existing contrast-based methods use the diagonal of the denoiser Jacobian, which reflects the posterior variance of each pixel. However, a small diagonal entry is ambiguous: it signals either memorization or averaging over many neighboring pixels in smooth or predictable regions. To resolve this ambiguity, these methods subtract a reference map, which requires a second evaluation with a null prompt or an earlier checkpoint. Unconditional models have no null prompt, and earlier checkpoints are unavailable in general. We show that Jacobian row sums (JaRS), unlike the diagonal, separate memorization from local averaging without a reference map. Pairing JaRS with an image-level detection score that uses the same statistic at an early denoising step yields JaRS+. Across Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.1, Realistic Vision v5.1, and an unconditional diffusion Transformer (DiT), JaRS+ outperforms contrast-based localization methods.

items.title: A Generalizable Approach to Safety-Aware Robotic Behavior Planning with an Explicit Constraint Space
items.description: arXiv:2611.18026v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language and vision-language models have substantially advanced robotic behavior planning from natural-language instructions and visual observations. However, safe manipulation in tabletop environments remains challenging because the safety constraints required for a task depend on the surrounding scene and may not be explicitly specified in the instruction. We propose a safety-aware behavior planning framework based on an explicit Constraint Space that stores reusable textual safety rules. Rather than retrieving rules solely by semantic similarity, we formulate constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning. A lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model identifies the constraints applicable to the current context, which are then provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. To handle incorrect constraint selections and previously unseen hazards, we introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that evaluates generated primitive plans, reconstructs the complete applicable constraint set, and provides corrective planning feedback. Validated inspection feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of constraint applicability and parameter-efficient adaptation of the Safety Inspector through LoRA, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space. The resulting framework integrates explicit safety knowledge representation,context-aware constraint selection, corrective safety inspection, and test-time knowledge adaptation for safety-aware robotic behavior planning.

items.title: Beyond Bot Labels: Retrospective Consequence-Grounded Ranking of Attributed Cache Harm in E-Commerce Logs
items.description: arXiv:2611.18027v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Web caches reduce origin load and latency, but automated traffic can either warm them or evict objects shoppers reuse, lowering the cache hit ratio (CHR). Existing bot defenses generally infer automation from User-Agent (UA) strings or behavior rather than identify sessions that impose cross-session cache harm. We instead formulate the task as ranking sessions by eviction damage and propose consequence-grounded session ranking. A single chronological replay attributes each eviction-induced miss by a protected shopping session (a victim) to the session whose insertion last evicted the object. A behavioral model predicts the target from session behavior alone. Selected sessions bypass the cache but remain origin-served. In a controlled check of 539 non-victim sessions selected across harm levels, attribution order tracks victim-hit changes after removal (Spearman correlation 0.80). On a 12.7-million-request real trace, the top 1% of sessions carry 48.8% of attributed harm. Sessions without bot tags contribute 49.1% of this tier's harm. At the 20% request-volume target, the default conditional CHR difference reaches 93% of the UA baseline, which selects 47 times as many sessions. Six training seeds show little variation. This comparison conditions on the victims that remain, so we also report victim bypass. Local replay and retraining on a second store reproduce harm concentration and a top tier dominated by sessions without bot tags. These results establish attributed cross-session harm as an outcome-based target for retrospective cache audits and selective intervention design.

items.title: Product units in gated recurrent networks enhance prediction of nuclear masses and charge radii
items.description: arXiv:2611.18066v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The prediction of nuclear properties using machine learning can complement theoretical models and advance the exploration of poorly known domains of the nuclear chart. We propose a machine learning technique for predicting nuclear masses and charge radii based on gated recurrent units (GRU) that integrates learnable product-unit mappings into the candidate state to model multiplicative dependencies among neighboring nuclei. Computations are performed in the complex domain to jointly capture amplitude and phase dynamics. Across three data partitions and three training seeds per partition, AM-PU-GRU achieves a mean mass interpolation RMSE of 0.2698 MeV and a temporal RMSE of 0.1905 MeV. Configuration comparisons support the integration of learned products into gated recurrence. Without mass inputs, MI-PU-GRU predicts charge radii with an RMSE of 0.019947 fm, 14.40% below the fixed WS* prior. Matched radius controls further show how candidate fusion shapes the benefit of learned products. Paired errors, nuclide-resolved maps, and inference measurements characterize predictive gains and computational cost. This article is an extended version of our ICCS 2026 conference paper (doi:10.1007/978-3-032-29921-5_10).

items.title: Training-point consistency of kernel ridge regression with varying correlation scales
items.description: arXiv:2611.18095v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The scale parameter in kernel ridge regression plays a pivotal role in modeling the correlation structure of data. In modern applications, sampling density and the underlying correlation range often change simultaneously, making a fixed-scale assumption highly restrictive. However, establishing asymptotic theories under varying scale parameters is fundamentally challenging. To address this gap, this paper develops a unified theoretical framework for kernel ridge regression under varying scale parameters. We establish that, on uniform tensor grids with product exponential kernels, the consistency of the training-point risk holds if and only if the effective local sample size diverges to infinity. This sharp criterion universally covers all regimes along arbitrary deterministic scale sequences, seamlessly unifying the long-range, fixed-scale, and short-range. Furthermore, we provide an explicit, signal-independent construction of a deterministic regularization penalty that guarantees this consistency. Numerical experiments illustrate the criterion and the corresponding penalty across all the three regimes.

items.title: Muon Attains $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ Iteration Complexity under Shuffling
items.description: arXiv:2611.18124v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Muon is a stochastic first-order optimizer for matrix-valued parameters. It maintains an exponential moving average of stochastic gradients in a momentum buffer with coefficient $\beta$, and orthogonalizes the buffer to obtain the update direction. Muon has been reported to accelerate and stabilize the training of large language models. In practice, it is often used with shuffling (sampling without replacement), where each epoch visits the components of a finite-sum objective in a permuted order. However, its iteration complexity in this setting remains open. We analyze Muon under shuffling, with the momentum buffer orthogonalized by the polar map. For smooth nonconvex finite-sum problems, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ iteration complexity for finding an $\varepsilon$-stationary point. This guarantee holds for every sequence of permutations, covering random reshuffling, shuffle once, and the incremental gradient method. This complexity matches that of stochastic gradient descent under shuffling in its dependence on $\varepsilon$, and improves on Muon's $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ complexity under sampling with replacement. Our guarantee requires a problem-dependent $\beta$ that approaches one as the number of components grows. In contrast, no fixed $\beta$ guarantees convergence to stationarity for every number of components. We show this by constructing a family of smooth convex problems on which, for any fixed $\beta\in[0,1)$, Muon remains bounded away from stationarity once the number of components is sufficiently large. This failure occurs for every sequence of permutations and persists even with small stepsizes. These results suggest two practical tuning rules: if the training loss stops decreasing even after reducing the stepsize, increase $\beta$; when increasing $\beta$, reduce the stepsize accordingly.

items.title: PRISM: A Post-Prediction Reliability Framework for Evidence-Guided Correction and Selective Abstention
items.description: arXiv:2611.18127v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A model may produce a prediction with high confidence and still get the outcome wrong. This is a challenge in sequential applications, where the system evolves over time and deployment data may differ from the data used during training. To address this issue, we propose PRISM (Prediction Reliability and Intelligent Self-Correction Mechanism), a framework that evaluates prediction reliability after the initial output is generated. It estimates the risk of error and examines predictions identified as potentially unreliable. For these cases, PRISM analyses available signals, retrieves similar situations from historical data, and verifies whether an alternative prediction is supported by the evidence. It can then retain the original prediction, apply a verified correction, or abstain when the evidence is insufficient. We evaluate PRISM on second-innings match prediction in the Indian Premier League (IPL). Ball-by-ball records are converted into over-level observations to capture changes in match conditions throughout an innings. To preserve temporal order, earlier IPL seasons are used for training, IPL 2024 for validation, and IPL 2025-2026 for out-of-time testing. The dataset contains 8,665 over-level observations from 475 matches, with the test partition comprising 2,568 observations from 142 matches. In one experimental record, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and HistGradientBoosting achieve accuracies of 65.2%, 68.4%, and 70.2%, respectively. The corresponding PRISM evaluation reports a selective accuracy of 82.4% at 88.5% coverage, with a Brier score of 0.126 and an expected calibration error (ECE) of 0.019.

items.title: Compiling Specialized GPU-Initiated Networking
items.description: arXiv:2611.18145v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning systems specialize computation to the workload and hardware, but communication remains in generic libraries whose device code and transport decisions are not visible to high-level compilers. We present Obaleth, a compiler that makes GPU-initiated communication part of a kernel's intermediate representation, co-optimizes it alongside computation, and lowers it to specialized transport code. Obaleth plans completions around buffer lifetimes and optimizes memory ordering, synchronization, and batching across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. On H100 GPUs, Obaleth sends small messages up to 3.3$\times$ faster, and on 256 GPUs runs all-to-all 1.25$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ faster than NVSHMEM and NCCL GIN, with much smaller memory and register use. In vLLM, it serves Qwen3-235B on 16 B200 GPUs and answers requests up to 1.29$\times$ faster than with DeepEP.

items.title: Detection and Classification in Latent Spaces: High-Dimensional Analysis and Validation
items.description: arXiv:2611.18164v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Foundation models produce high-dimensional latent representations in which suitably designed statistical decision rules can be effective yet analytically tractable. We study such detectors in the high-dimensional regime, where latent dimension and training sample size grow proportionally. For linear and quadratic statistics, we derive explicit large-deviation characterizations of false-alarm and miss-detection performance under the Neyman-Pearson paradigm, and show how the binary analysis extends to multi-class classification. The resulting error probabilities and corresponding decay rates exhibit non-monotonic dependence on the shape parameter, including double-descent and, in some regimes, multiple-descent. Experiments on vision, text, and audio datasets using modern foundation models show close agreement between theoretical predictions and empirical performance. In particular, the proposed framework allows us to set a prescribed false-alarm level and accurately predict the corresponding miss-detection probability. Overall, our results provide a theoretically grounded and interpretable framework with competitive empirical performance across different modalities.

items.title: LaMe: a Joint Latent Mediation Framework for High-Dimensional Systems
items.description: arXiv:2611.18180v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mediation analysis seeks to understand how an exposure influences an outcome through intermediate variables. However, as increasingly rich datasets become available, hundreds to thousands of potential mediators make these systems difficult to model and hard to interpret. Latent-variable approaches offer a natural way to accommodate these high-dimensional settings. However, existing latent mediation methods face limitations, including overparameterization, biased inference, or limited scalability. We develop LaMe, a joint linear-Gaussian framework that summarizes a high-dimensional exposure-mediator-outcome system through a small number of latent variables. We identify natural direct and indirect effects under an explicit assumption that the manifest measurements fully capture the latent mediators, and characterize conditions under which the latent representation effectively restricts the observed cross-covariance structure. Simulations assess recovery of observed association parameters, natural effects, and manifest features associated with latent mediation pathways across a range of challenging settings. Four real-world applications demonstrate competitive predictive performance with compact latent representations, including single-dimensional representations of biomarker and proteomic measurements. Together, these results establish LaMe as a practical framework for estimating and summarizing multivariate mediation systems under explicit structural and measurement assumptions.

items.title: Online Switching Control as Learning with Experts
items.description: arXiv:2611.18352v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of online switching control for discrete-time nonlinear systems where a controller is sequentially selected from a finite set of candidates. The goal is to generate an adaptive sequence of controllers to minimize the cumulative cost under unknown disturbances and cost functions. Specifically, we consider a full-information feedback setting where realized disturbance effects and cost functions are available after each selection. Using counterfactual costs computed from historical data, we reduce the online switching control problem to the experts problem with switching costs. Then, we propose an adaptive switching algorithm based on the Hedge algorithm with a switching suppression mechanism. Notably, the proposed algorithm achieves an expected regret of $O(\sqrt{T\log N})$, where $T$ is the time horizon and $N$ is the number of candidate controllers, while ensuring uniform boundedness of the state. This matches the optimal regret order for the standard experts problem.

items.title: Adaptable Watermarking: Transforming Image Watermarking Models via Lightweight Adapters
items.description: arXiv:2611.18363v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We explore the adaptability of neural image watermarking models; the extent to which one watermarking method can be transformed into another through lightweight adaptation. We introduce a framework that enables encoder-decoder watermarking architectures to become modular and upgradable, supporting multiple watermarking styles without re-training full models. Adaptation is performed by attaching a compact parameter-efficient adapter and fine-tuning under a multi-domain residual alignment loss (spatial, gradient, and frequency) while preserving bit accuracy via a secret-loss term. We evaluate this approach across a suite of recent watermarking models, including TrustMark, InvisMark, RoSteALS, HiDDeN, and WAM, demonstrating that adapted encoders closely reproduce target residuals and that adapted decoders recover messages with near-optimal accuracy under standard augmentations and distortions. We show that cross-model adaptation, with applications in interoperable and upgradable watermarking, can be achieved with as few as 1-2M trainable parameters per component (e.g., the 2M decoder adapter used in our multi-decoder inference pipeline).

items.title: Structure makes quantum circuits trainable
items.description: arXiv:2611.18378v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The scalability of variational quantum algorithms is limited by barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially in system size. This worst-case result raises fundamental questions about the trainability of quantum AI models. We present a major advance towards resolving this trainability question by answering whether a given quantum circuit has a barren plateau. We do this using an analytical framework that bounds the gradient variance for arbitrary input states $\rho$ and observables $\mathcal{M}$ by decomposing the unitary representation of the associated compact Lie group. When the circuit segments on both sides of a gate form $2$-designs, we obtain the variance exactly and prove a sufficient condition for trainability: if $\rho^{\otimes 2}$ and $\mathcal{M}^{\otimes 2}$ are sufficiently concentrated on the same irreducible invariant subspace of polynomial dimension, and the differentiated gate moves this subspace by an inverse-polynomial amount, then the gradient variance is at least inverse-polynomial. We further present a sampling algorithm that estimates the gradient variance from runs of the ansatz, without constructing the representation-theoretic projectors. Our algorithm decides whether the variance exceeds a tolerance $\tau$ with the number of runs polynomial in $1/\tau$, including cases in which the bounds are inconclusive. This resolves the question of the trainability of the circuit before expensive training procedures.

items.title: A systematic comparison of physics-informed neural networks and mechanistic models for epidemic modeling and forecasting
items.description: arXiv:2611.18389v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently been applied to epidemic modeling and forecasting with promising results. These methods integrate mechanistic knowledge with data-driven learning. Yet, their comparative performance against well-established, and simpler epidemic models is underexplored. Here, we conduct a systematic comparison of a PINN-based framework and a stochastic mechanistic model. Both approaches share the same age-structured SEIRD core and rolling-window forecasting pipeline, in a deliberately minimal setting. We evaluate their retrospective fits and probabilistic forecasts in two synthetic scenarios and the first COVID-19 wave in London. Interestingly, while PINNs underperform in synthetic scenarios, they achieve better performance on real data. Furthermore, PINNs provide narrower uncertainty intervals and sharper estimation of parameters in synthetic scenarios. Our findings confirm PINNs as a promising tool in epidemiology. At the same time, the results reaffirm the value of simpler approaches such as traditional compartmental models, and promote additional benchmarking studies.

items.title: Lipschitz-Constrained Discriminators in Generative Modeling: Asymptotic Behavior and Support Mismatch
items.description: arXiv:2611.18394v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the asymptotic behavior of optimal discriminators associated to $L-$Lipschitz regularized KL-divergences of two probability distributions $Q$ and $P$ that interpolate between the rescaled Wasserstein$-1$ metric by some parameter $L>0$ and the KL divergence. The parameter $L$ plays the role of a Lipschitz constraint and is viewed as a regularization parameter: small values of $L$ enforce a more geometry-aware discriminator, while as $L$ increases the geometric regularization is progressively relaxed. It is a known result [3] that such divergences converge to the KL divergence as $L\to\infty$. In this paper, we characterize the asymptotic behavior of the optimal discriminators as $L\to\infty$ in different regimes: Firstly, under $Q\ll P$ and the Radon-Nikodym derivative $\frac{dQ}{dP}$ is bounded from above and bounded away from zero. Secondly, when $Q$ and $P$ are discrete distributions satisfying $Q\ll P$, and finally when $Q$ and $P$ are non absolutely continuous discrete distributions. This result motivates training strategies which involve discriminators, such as adversarial generative models. In practice, the data distribution is often represented by a discrete empirical measure, while, especially at the early stages of the training, the model distribution may have little or no overlap with the empirical data distribution.

items.title: Graph diffusion transformer for interpretable generation and inverse design of disordered atomic structures
items.description: arXiv:2611.18420v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Atomic disorder offers a potent degree of freedom to tailor material properties, yet the resulting vast configuration space obscures structure-property relations and hinders rational inverse design. Here we introduce Graph Amorphous Diffusion Transformer (GaDiT), a generative model that combines dynamic periodic graphs, masked conditioning and an interval-weighted training-noise distribution. GaDiT generates high-quality disordered structures while accelerating sampling by two orders of magnitude compared with existing corrector-based approaches, as demonstrated across two-dimensional amorphous carbon and three-dimensional amorphous silicon and silica. Moreover, GaDiT supports conditional generation under single or combined structural features, physical properties and preparation conditions in a unified model, and enables inverse design that expands accessible structure-property ranges beyond the training distribution. To interpret these structures and the trained network, we propose a conditioned atomic response mapping analysis, revealing both the global structural descriptors and the local atomic environments that govern target properties. Overall, GaDiT establishes a general framework for interpretable generation, inverse design and structure-property discovery for disordered atomic structures.

items.title: The State Is Not the Bottleneck: A Paged-State Gated-DeltaNet Tile on a Tri-Mode Multicast Mesh, Bit-Exact from RTL to Silicon
items.description: arXiv:2611.18422v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Linear-attention language models replace a growing key-value cache with a recurrent state of fixed size. On an edge FPGA, this state can exceed the on-chip memory and must be paged to external memory. This paper asks whether such paging dominates the cost of decoding (generating tokens). We built a hardware tile that computes one complete layer of a custom 369-million-parameter hybrid Gated DeltaNet model on an Agilex 5 FPGA and pages its recurrent state. The model state needs 6.2 MiB, whereas the device has 0.87 MiB of block memory. Paging adds 26.0 MB of memory traffic per decoded token, at most 11.2 percent of the calculated total. On the board at 75 MHz, with synthetic weights, one token takes 11.15 ms in this layer. The matrix-vector products with the weights take about 62 percent of this time and the state phase, including the paging, 13 percent. The tile is one node of a multicast mesh of tri-mode processing elements. We measure the error of the fixed-point arithmetic against floating point and check that the hardware agrees bit for bit with a fixed-point reference. In simulation, the state logic agrees with the reference on all 18 recurrent layers. On the board, six builds pass all 30 runs of 64 tokens and two runs of 1,024 tokens. For this model and memory interface, the delivery of the weights limits the decoding performance, and the recurrent state does not. State paging is therefore practical for such a model on an edge FPGA.

items.title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
items.description: arXiv:2611.18459v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.

items.title: Contrastive latent representation learning with denoising score matching
items.description: arXiv:2611.18469v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Contrastive representation learning methods operate by pulling different views of the same data sample together while pushing them away from views of different samples. A fundamental challenge is the estimation of the repulsive force, which typically requires large batch sizes, can exhibit high variance, and is susceptible to the curse of dimensionality. We introduce ScoreCLR, a contrastive representation learning method that offers a novel way to estimate this repulsion term. We consider the framework of representation learning by maximizing the mutual information between two latent views of a sample. By deriving the gradient of the Shannon entropy with respect to the encoder parameters, we obtain an equivalent objective that involves the score of the latent representation. We then use denoising score matching techniques to estimate this score with a lightweight network that is trained jointly with the encoder. We further propose regularization techniques using different noise levels and a Gaussian prior on the latent representation. ScoreCLR replaces the batch of explicit negative samples in contrastive methods with a learned repulsion whose cost is linear in the batch size rather than quadratic. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 it does so with minimal loss of linear-probe accuracy compared to SimCLR under a shared recipe, while producing projector outputs of higher effective rank, closer to the Gaussian prior.

items.title: Evaluating Feedback-Driven Black-Box Processes via Stochastic Modeling and Simulation
items.description: arXiv:2611.18477v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study feedback-driven black-box processes across software engineering and machine learning. These processes are inherently sequential: policies generate inputs, observe outputs/feedback from systems, and use the feedback to guide the design of subsequent inputs. While many policies are developed under structural assumptions on the underlying systems, many real-world systems operate without such knowledge, necessitating black-box policies that lack a unified evaluation framework. We introduce a stochastic framework that models and evaluates such policies using Markov chains and simulation, thereby connecting empirical practice with theory. We instantiate the framework in mutation-based fuzzing (widely used for discovering software bugs via sequential input mutation), by a novel Markov chain model of fuzzing whose transitions are governed by the mutation strategy and whose feedback is given by program execution. We develop a rigorous evaluation paradigm with new performance measures, sound estimators, and evaluation procedures with provable guarantees. Guided by the theory, we evaluate 9 fuzzers on 18 widely used fuzzing benchmarks and conduct case studies in 4 non-fuzzing domains. These results show that the framework provides a principled basis for evaluation while connecting to practice, with implications beyond fuzzing.

items.title: Bregman geometry in regular exponential families: dual representations and relative smoothness
items.description: arXiv:2611.18480v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Regular exponential-family distributions are ubiquitous in statistics due to their appealing and convenient properties. Notably, they can be expressed in terms of Bregman divergences, revealing fundamental connections between statistics, convex analysis, and information geometry. However, this geometric structure has not been systematically exploited to characterize these distributions with respect to their expectation parametrization. Building on a projective characterization, we establish a general construction of equivalent dual Bregman representations, together with normalization and uniqueness results. These representations express log-densities as ordinary Bregman divergences in dual coordinate systems, providing geometric characterizations of the parameter space. So-called $\beta$- and $\alpha$-scaled dual representations emerge as particular instances of this framework. We further derive dual Bregman representations of conjugate priors and establish that they preserve conjugacy. Applications to classical distributions illustrate the geometric structures underlying seemingly different statistical models. Moreover, we show that these representations provide natural reference geometries for establishing relative smoothness of the primal Bregman representation of the distribution, with explicit bounds that are sharp in the scalar and separable settings. An illustrative application to the Poisson distribution sheds new light on several works in the literature, providing complementary geometric justifications for reference geometries while deriving existing algorithms.

items.title: StreamEmbed: Real-Time Indexing from Pixels for Screenshot Retrieval
items.description: arXiv:2611.18516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Screen history can serve as searchable visual memory for people and agents, but unlike an offline corpus, it must be encoded and indexed as each screenshot arrives. OCR-based indexing is fast but loses visual information; visual encoding takes over two seconds. Yet screens change incrementally: most pixels repeat within and across screenshots. This raises a question: do visual encoders need to recompute their representations from scratch for every new screenshot? We present StreamEmbed, a system for incremental visual embedding that exploits this redundancy. Guided solely by pixel differences, it combines spatial token pruning, which skips blocks that repeat a neighbor, with temporal KV reuse, which reuses cached keys and values for blocks unchanged across screenshots. A small learned adapter compensates for pruning and reuse to preserve fidelity to full-screenshot embeddings. On ScreenMemEval, our benchmark of 10,426 questions over 184 hours of screen histories from two humans and a computer-use agent, StreamEmbed sets a new accuracy-latency Pareto frontier on an M2 Pro GPU: it encodes up to 3.7x faster than full-screenshot encoding without sacrificing accuracy and improves accuracy over OCR-based indexing by up to 6.3 Recall@10 points at matched latency. A memory-efficient vector index stores a simulated year of screenshots in 0.13 GB of RAM. Together, these results make real-time indexing of screen history in its native visual form practical, laying a foundation for fully local visual assistants.

items.title: Understanding Contextual Bias in Agricultural CNNs Through Hidden-Neuron Concept Induction
items.description: arXiv:2611.18530v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can classify images using background-dominated patches that contain little or none of the target object, showing that they exploit contextual information. Previous studies detected this behavior through classification accuracy but say little about what CNN hidden layers represent. We investigate whether Concept Induction can reveal interpretable visual properties associated with hidden-neuron activations on contextual image patches. Using five agricultural datasets with high, moderate, and low contextual bias, we analyze four CNN architectures at three network depths and five patch locations. Quantitative image descriptors of each patch are encoded in a knowledge graph and used as background knowledge for Concept Induction, which derives logical expressions characterizing neuron activation. These expressions are tested on held-out images using the Mann-Whitney U test and Cliff's delta. Of 48,013 tested neuron-feature pairs, 13,164 (27.4%) were validated. Validation was most frequent at intermediate depths (mean 40.2% at mid layers versus 12.0% at deep layers), and no patch location dominated across datasets. Among the tested descriptors, edge, Gabor, and Tamura texture features had the highest validation rates. Stronger contextual bias did not correspond to higher neuron-feature validation rates: moderately biased Sugarcane had the highest rate (40.5%) and highly biased Cassava the lowest (19.2%). These results suggest that behavioral context dependence and the semantic interpretability of hidden neurons capture different aspects of CNN behavior, and that Concept Induction can complement patch-based bias detection.

items.title: Why Finite Intelligence Works in an Infinite World: A Mathematical Theory
items.description: arXiv:2611.18538v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An information system often has to learn before it knows what it will be asked. A finite representation can succeed without recording an infinite environment in full when those asks share collective structure, rather than demand unrelated facts scattered arbitrarily across it. We formalize this phenomenon through future-task information, the minimum retained information needed to preserve decision value relative to the available evidence. A joint decision-regret state records posterior comparisons among actions for every permitted task. Under compactness assumptions, every retained representation admits a calibrated replacement based on this state, preserving all task regrets without increasing information; the resulting information-regret curve equals an operational coding rate. Two exact boundaries govern finite preservation: weak-star closure for a fixed action count, and the singular mass of the source-evidence law when all finite action menus are admitted. Collective structure determines information requirements beyond individual-question difficulty. Families with identical source laws, pairwise task metrics, and individual-task rates can have different high-resolution exponents. Covariance-identical coordinate and parity families have different exact rate-distortion curves, with optimal parity retention characterized by a sharp Fourier-entropy inequality. For balanced nested task families, refinement sizes and weighted reach determine the rate within an additive constant, attained by prefix coding under explicit decay conditions. Nonlinear learning and computational separations distinguish preservation from efficient discovery and use. The proposed mathematical theory identifies which shared decision requirements allow finite information to remain useful for infinitely many possible purposes.

items.title: BAL: Bidirectional Autoregression in Latent Space for Learning Human Movement Representations
items.description: arXiv:2611.18559v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference. To suppress representation collapse, BAL decomposes each prediction target into a global component capturing sequence-level semantics and a local component capturing context-independent movement. We prove that the local targets retain nontrivial angular diversity unless the representations are completely collapsed, preserving a meaningful training signal. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that BAL's representations are highly effective for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most evaluation metrics.

items.title: FETTUCCINE: Fast and efficient brain-to-text decoding on mobile devices
items.description: arXiv:2611.18561v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in speech neuroprostheses have enabled new communication avenues for people who have lost the ability to speak due to neurological illness or injury. These systems can decode neural activity during attempted speech into text by relying on language priors to achieve high decoding accuracy. This performance currently comes at the cost of using a compute-intensive language modeling stack, presenting a major bottleneck for real-world use. Further, current language models incur highly variable and disruptive inference latencies, limiting communication throughput and preventing users from reliably participating in natural conversation. We introduce FETTUCCINE, an end-to-end brain-to-text framework that leverages the speed and portability of automatic speech recognition (ASR) models to address the aforementioned practical challenges, while achieving usable (<10%) word error rates (WER), efficient adaptation to neural non-stationarities, and reliable performance on mobile devices. When evaluated using publicly available data from an intracortical speech neuroprosthesis user, FETTUCCINE outperforms previous end-to-end methods, achieving as low as 4.39% WER. Most notably, our models successfully run on a commercially-available mobile device with throughput reaching up to 370x real-time, providing the first demonstration of brain-to-text decoding on a mobile device. We also show that our models can be successfully finetuned to extend usable performance to future days. Beyond performance, our approach enables localization of the neural features most relevant for decoding via gradient-based saliency maps, which we show align with well-established physiological priors across different ASR model families. Taken together, our results show that FETTUCCINE overcomes core infrastructural and computational barriers, yielding a new class of portable brain-to-text communication.

items.title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
items.description: arXiv:2611.18562v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $\pi_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $\pi_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

items.title: Robust Long-Tailed Learning under Label Noise
items.description: arXiv:2108.11569v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-tailed learning aims to enhance the generalization performance of underrepresented tail classes. However, previous methods have largely overlooked the prevalence of noisy labels in training data. In this paper, we address the challenge of noisy labels in long-tailed learning. We identify a critical issue: the commonly used small-loss noisy label detection criterion fails to perform effectively in long-tailed class distributions. This failure arises from the inherent bias of deep neural networks, which tend to misclassify tail class examples as head classes, leading to unreliable loss calculations. To mitigate this, we propose a novel small-distance criterion that leverages the robustness of learned representations, enabling more accurate identification of correctly-labeled examples across both head and tail classes. Additionally, to improve training for tail classes, we replace discrete pseudo-labels with label distributions for examples flagged as noisy, resulting in significant performance gains. Based on these contributions, we introduce the Robust Long-Tail learning framework, designed to train models that are resilient to both class imbalance and noisy labels. Extensive experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms previous methods, offering substantial performance improvements.

items.title: Bidirectional Information Flow (BIF) - A Sample Efficient Hierarchical Gaussian Process for Bayesian Optimization
items.description: arXiv:2505.11294v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hierarchical Gaussian Process (H-GP) models divide problems into different subtasks, allowing for different components to address each part, making them well-suited for problems with inherent compositional structure. However, existing H-GP frameworks typically employ one-way information sharing - either top-down or bottom-up - which limits sample efficiency and slows convergence. We propose Bidirectional Information Flow (BIF), which establishes continuous two-way communication. BIF retains the modular structure of hierarchical models - the parent conditions its own posterior on child summaries, treating them as structured priors - while introducing top-down feedback to softly decompose environment observations from the parent into sub-responses. This mutual exchange improves sample efficiency, enables robust training, and allows modular reuse of learned subtask models. We prove analytically the regret of a GP with a learned kernel scales linearly with the mismatch to the true kernel, tightening in the hierarchical case to the sum of child-level errors. Ablation shows removing the downward pathway collapses child $R^2$ by up to 58%. Across synthetic, neurostimulation, and HPO benchmarks, BIF achieves up to $4\times$ higher parent $R^2$ and roughly 100% AUC improvement over vanilla GPBO, and outperforms or is the runner-up in 38/40 tests compared to the state-of-the-art baselines while supporting modular child transfer to novel composite tasks.

items.title: Robust Surrogate Modeling for Explainable Graph Neural Networks
items.description: arXiv:2508.01925v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable performance in a wide range of graph-related learning tasks. However, explaining their predictions remains a challenging problem, especially due to the mismatch between the graphs used during training and those encountered during explanation. Most existing methods optimize soft edge masks on weighted graphs to highlight important substructures, but these graphs differ from the unweighted graphs on which GNNs are trained. This distributional shift leads to unreliable gradients and degraded explanation quality, especially when generating small, sparse subgraphs. To address this issue, we propose explaining a robust surrogate whose explanations provide a faithful proxy for those of the original model. Specifically, we train this surrogate model through an iterative re-weighting strategy that alternates between identifying explanation subgraphs and adapting the model to the resulting weighted graph distribution, supporting stable explanation refinement while preserving the validity of the soft-mask relaxation. We evaluate our method on multiple benchmark datasets using different GNN backbones and explanation methods. Experimental results show that our method consistently improves explanation quality and can be flexibly integrated with different architectures.

items.title: Structured Basis Function Networks: Loss-Centric Multi-Hypothesis Ensembles with Controllable Diversity
items.description: arXiv:2509.02792v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ensemble learning and multi-hypothesis prediction are two complementary paradigms for improving predictive performance and robustness. This work introduces the Structured Basis Function Network (s-BFN), a loss-aware ensemble framework that unifies these paradigms through a supervised aggregation mechanism motivated by the loss-induced Bregman-centroid geometry of prediction space. The approach constructs a structured dataset of base predictions and trains a parametric combiner directly against the observed labels, with the centroidal formulation serving as a geometric reference rather than an exact centroid solver, while a diversity-control parameter regulates specialization among predictors. The proposed framework is evaluated across regression and classification tasks, including tabular data, image recognition, and large-scale temporally structured video classification. Empirical results show that s-BFN provides strong performance across the evaluated regimes and is competitive with the aggregation baselines considered in the study. The strongest gains are observed in higher-dimensional and temporally structured settings, where aggregation capacity and controlled diversity are jointly beneficial, while simpler tabular regimes exhibit earlier saturation. These results highlight a capacity-complexity-diversity trade-off rather than a strictly monotonic relationship between diversity, ensemble size, and accuracy.

items.title: Bayesian Transfer Operators in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
items.description: arXiv:2509.22482v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transfer operators provide a linear description of nonlinear dynamical systems by propagating observables or probability distributions. In reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, these operators are represented through conditional mean embeddings, whose regularized estimator coincides with the posterior mean of Gaussian process regression. Building on this correspondence, we formulate Gaussian Process Dynamic Mode Decomposition, a Bayesian transfer-operator method that combines sparse variational Gaussian processes with kernel-based Koopman and Perron--Frobenius operator approximation. The resulting framework provides a principled route to uncertainty quantification, scalable sparse approximations, and data-adaptive dictionary learning for prediction and spectral analysis. Additionally, the model-selection formulation naturally gives rise to a forward--backward operator structure, which establishes a connection between Bayesian transfer-operator learning and time-lagged canonical correlation analysis.

items.title: Simultaneous Learning and Optimization via Misspecified Saddle Point Problems
items.description: arXiv:2510.05241v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a class of misspecified saddle point (SP) problems, where the optimization objective depends on an unknown parameter that must be learned concurrently from data. Unlike existing studies that assume parameters are fully known or pre-estimated, our framework integrates optimization and learning into a unified formulation, enabling a more flexible problem class. To address this setting, we propose two algorithms based on the accelerated primal-dual (APD) by Hamedani & Aybat 2021. In particular, we first analyze the naive extension of the APD method by directly substituting the evolving parameter estimates into the primal-dual updates; then, we design a new learning-aware variant of the APD method that explicitly accounts for parameter dynamics by adjusting the momentum updates. Both methods achieve a provable convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(\log K / K)$, while the learning-aware approach attains a tighter $\mathcal{O}(1)$ constant and further benefits from an adaptive step-size selection enabled by a backtracking strategy. Furthermore, we extend the framework to problems where the learning problem admits multiple optimal solutions, showing that our modified algorithm for a structured setting achieves an $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K})$ rate. To demonstrate practical impact, we evaluate our methods on a misspecified portfolio optimization problem and show superior empirical performance compared to state-of-the-art algorithms.

items.title: Adversarial Attacks on Downstream Weather Forecasting Models: Application to Tropical Cyclone Trajectory Prediction
items.description: arXiv:2510.10140v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep learning-based weather forecasting (DLWF) models leverage past weather observations to generate future forecasts, supporting a wide range of downstream applications, including tropical cyclone (TC) prediction. In this paper, we investigate the vulnerability of these models to adversarial attacks, where subtle perturbations to upstream forecasts can alter downstream TC trajectory predictions. Crafting perturbed inputs to steer downstream outputs toward attacker-specified trajectories is a challenging problem for several reasons. First, conventional TC detection systems are opaque, non-differentiable black boxes, making standard gradient-based attacks infeasible. Second, the extreme rarity of TC events leads to a severe class imbalance problem, making it difficult to develop attack methods that produce realistic-looking cyclone paths aligned with target trajectories. To overcome these limitations, we propose Cyc-Attack, a novel method for perturbing the forecasts of DLWF models to generate adversarial trajectories. The proposed method uses a differentiable surrogate model to approximate the TC detector's output, enabling the application of gradient-based attacks. Cyc-Attack also employs a skewness-aware loss function with a kernel dilation strategy to address the severe class imbalance problem. Distance-based gradient weighting and regularization strategies are also introduced to constrain perturbations to eliminate unrealistic-looking TC paths. Our experiments show that Cyc-Attack achieves a higher true positive rate in matching the target trajectories, along with lower false alarm rates and stealthier perturbations than conventional attack methods. We further demonstrate that the adversarial upstream forecasts generated by Cyc-Attack can be leveraged as initial guidance to train an end-to-end model for learning adversarial input samples that would induce target trajectories.

items.title: CS-54k: A Paper-Grounded Corpus and Benchmark for AI Research QA
items.description: arXiv:2510.20279v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to support computer science research. To contribute reliably, these systems must be able to work with information distributed across research papers and across different aspects of the research process. However, large-scale resources that systematically organize such information into structured supervision for both model evaluation and post-training remain limited. To address this gap, we propose a systematic paper-to-QA construction pipeline that organizes information from AI research papers into structured QA pairs supported by source evidence. Using this pipeline, we construct CS-54k, a 54k-pair corpus derived from 14,474 openly licensed AI research papers. The corpus covers eight recurring paper components, including research domain, prior work, existing challenges, motivation, findings and assumptions, methods, experimental settings, and experimental results. We further derive two complementary subsets: CS-4k, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on paper-derived research QA, and CS-50k, a companion corpus for post-training. Extensive evaluations on CS-4k reveal substantial performance differences across existing LLMs and paper components, with experimental settings and results remaining particularly challenging. Moreover, post-training on CS-50k substantially improves Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on CS-4k, demonstrating the practical utility of structured, paper-derived supervision. Together, CS-4k and CS-50k provide a unified and scalable resource for benchmarking and improving LLMs on research paper question answering.

items.title: Amortized Inference of Multi-Modal Posteriors using Likelihood-Weighted Normalizing Flows
items.description: arXiv:2512.04954v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a technique for posterior estimation using Normalizing Flows trained with likelihood-weighted importance sampling, the special case of neural importance sampling in which the proposal is the prior. This approach allows for the efficient inference of theoretical parameters in high-dimensional inverse problems without the need for posterior training samples. We implement the method on multi-modal benchmark tasks in 2D and 3D to check for the efficacy. A critical observation of our study is the impact of the base distribution on the modelled posteriors. We find that standard unimodal base distributions leave spurious probability \textit{bridges} between well-separated modes. We demonstrate that initializing the flow with a Gaussian Mixture Model that matches the number of target modes significantly improves reconstruction fidelity, as measured by some distance and divergence metrics. Finally, we apply this method to a curated problem in heavy flavour physics --- the extraction of the Wolfenstein parameters from the CP asymmetry in $B^0\to J/\psi\,K^0$; it is multimodal, non-Gaussian, and asymmetric in its mode weights --- and compare the results against a well-converged Markov Chain Monte Carlo reference and an exact reference computed by quadrature, using different metrics. Used as a proposal for importance sampling, the trained flow removes its remaining bias and gives the evidence.

items.title: Improving Matrix Exponential for Generative AI Flows: A Taylor-Based Approach Beyond Paterson--Stockmeyer
items.description: arXiv:2512.20777v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The matrix exponential is a fundamental operator in scientific computing and system simulation, with applications ranging from control theory and quantum mechanics to modern generative machine learning. While Pad\'e approximants combined with scaling and squaring have long served as the standard, recent Taylor-based methods, which utilize polynomial evaluation schemes that surpass the classical Paterson--Stockmeyer technique, offer superior accuracy and reduced computational complexity. This paper presents an optimized Taylor-based algorithm for the matrix exponential, specifically designed for the high-throughput requirements of generative AI flows. We provide a rigorous error analysis and develop a dynamic selection strategy for the Taylor order and scaling factor to minimize computational effort under a prescribed error tolerance. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that our approach provides significant acceleration and maintains high numerical stability compared to existing state-of-the-art implementations. These results establish the proposed method as a highly efficient tool for large-scale generative modeling.

items.title: Deep Multivariate Models with Parametric Conditionals
items.description: arXiv:2602.01953v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider deep multivariate models for heterogeneous collections of random variables. In the context of computer vision, such collections may e.g. consist of images, segmentations, image attributes, and latent variables. When developing such models, most existing works start from an application task and design the model components and their dependencies to meet the needs of the chosen task. This has the disadvantage of limiting the applicability of the resulting model for other downstream tasks. Here, instead, we propose to represent the joint probability distribution by means of conditional probability distributions for each group of variables conditioned on the rest. Such models can then be used for practically any possible downstream task. Their learning can be approached as training a parametrised Markov chain kernel by maximising the data likelihood of its limiting distribution. This has the additional advantage of allowing a wide range of semi-supervised learning scenarios.

items.title: Flow Matching from Viewpoint of Proximal Operators
items.description: arXiv:2602.12683v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We discuss the dynamics of Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) under the manifold hypothesis, where the support of the target distribution is a low dimensional manifold. We first derive an exact proximal expression of the vector field, using an extended Brenier potential for the OT; the vector field can be expressed by a denoiser, which is presented as the proximal operator associated with the potential function. Based on this explicit proximal form of the vector field, we analyze the manifold stability for perturbations to initial points, using the Lyapunov exponents of the dynamics. By analyzing the local behavior with the tools in convex analysis, we show that the dynamics contract linearly in the perturbation of the normal directions to the manifold, while perturbations in the tangential directions are preserved; this implies the stability of the manifold structure to the perturbations. To justify the theoretical arguments on the population OT, we also establish the convergence of minibatch OT-CFM with neural network learning to population OT-CFM under regularity and stability assumptions, with rate exponents governed by the intrinsic dimension of the data manifold. Experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10 support the predicted geometric behavior.

items.title: Denoising the US Census: Succinct Block Hierarchical Regression
items.description: arXiv:2603.10099v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The 2020 United States Census adopted differential privacy to protect individual confidentiality, adding calibrated noise to summary demographic measurements that are then reconciled into population tables. We developed BlueDown, a postprocessing algorithm that combines techniques from linear regression and constrained optimization while exploiting measurement structure for efficiency. On 2020 Census data, BlueDown reduced the error of groupings by race at the county level by 21-36% and of all county-level groupings by 9-58%; at the tract level, it reduced error of groupings by housing type by 38-61%. These gains came at no cost to confidentiality or computational efficiency, and would improve the validity of research relying on this definitive dataset and analyses used to guide the distribution of over $1.5 trillion in annual federal spending.

items.title: Resolving AdaBoost Cycling with LLMs: A Computer-Assisted Counterexample
items.description: arXiv:2604.07055v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a computer-assisted counterexample to the open question of whether exhaustive AdaBoost always converges to a finite cycle, posed by Rudin, Schapire, and Daubechies in COLT 2012. The construction is based on a block-product of two small AdaBoost instances whose two factors share an exact period-2 orbit for their five-step branch maps, but whose linearized return maps have dominant eigenvalues with an irrational logarithmic ratio. This irrationality forces the sequence of instances that win each round of updates to have an irrational asymptotic frequency, which precludes convergence to a finite cycle. The resulting counterexample has 2,500 examples, weak-learning margin $1/5$, and a uniform initial distribution, and it holds under every maximizing tie rule. All finite computations in the proof are certified by rational arithmetic in SymPy, with SageMath verifying the main inequalities. We also document the collaborative workflow that led to the construction, in which GPT-5.4 Pro produced the key technical arguments; Claude Opus 4.6 summarized and critiqued different versions of that work, proposing new directions to pursue; and the authors orchestrated the process by selecting directions to prioritize, resolving ambiguities, refining each argument, and verifying the final solution. Later conversations with GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra substantially simplified the solution. We present this as one of the first in-depth case studies of LLM-assisted mathematical research, resolving a long-standing open problem from theoretical machine learning, and detail the advantages and challenges of such research.

items.title: Retrieval of Coastal Biogeochemical Parameters From Near-Surface Hyperspectral Remote Sensing Reflectance Using Physics-Aware Meta-Learning
items.description: arXiv:2605.05623v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hyperspectral in situ sensing has shown promise in retrieving aquatic water quality (WQ) parameters, such as total suspended solids (TSS), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and total chlorophyll-a (TChl-a), for cost-effective management of coastal WQ. However, generalising such retrieval algorithms across water bodies remains challenging, as the relationship between remote sensing reflectance ($R_{rs}$) and WQ parameters can vary considerably from one region to another due to regional distinctions in environmental conditions and biogeochemistry that lead to different WQ ranges and bio-optical properties. In this study, we propose a two-stage physics-aware meta-learning framework for retrieving coastal WQ parameters from near-surface $R_{rs}$ observations. Unlike purely data-driven approaches trained solely on paired observations, the proposed framework incorporates physical knowledge through a two-stage learning process. In the first stage, a region-agnostic base model is pretrained using meta-learning on synthetic WQ--$R_{rs}$ samples generated by a bio-optical forward model parameterised with an in situ bio-optical spectral library. In the second stage, the pretrained model is fine-tuned using local samples to adapt to regional conditions. To evaluate the proposed approach, we collected in situ hyperspectral $R_{rs}$ and WQ measurements from five geographically distinct sites in Australian coastal waters.

items.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Domain Shift in Permission-Based Android Malware Detection
items.description: arXiv:2605.09028v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine learning-based Android malware detectors often fail in real-world deployment due to domain shift, where models trained on one data source perform poorly on applications from another. This paper presents a comprehensive study on the generalizability and interpretability of permission-based detectors under cross-domain conditions. Using two complementary datasets (PerMalDroid and NATICUSdroid) and five ensemble classifiers, we first establish an intra-domain baseline, where models achieve over 92% accuracy, and then quantify a severe asymmetric performance drop. While models trained on PerMalDroid generalize well to NATICUSdroid (86% accuracy), the reverse direction sees a drastic drop to 73% accuracy. Explainable AI analysis reveals bimodal feature distributions and shows that feature importance is highly unstable, with key permissions losing or gaining influence across domains.
